🔐 API Security/Functional Testing Architecture & Flow Diagrams

🛡️ Post-run gates — judging the RUN, not its assertions (KS-517 · KS-684)

Gates run after a Schemathesis sweep and feed the exit code alongside the check results (run validity, NDJSON completeness, report reconciliation, triaged baseline, plus the authenticated-coverage gate). They exist because every assertion-based gate shares one blind spot: a check that never ran cannot fail, so a run that tested nothing scores clean everywhere. Each of these answers “did this run have the standing to say anything?” rather than “what did it say?”
The gates — and how the sweep’s own exit code is read (KS-1408)
StatusGate / checkWhat it does
LiveAuthenticated coverage (KS-517)a sweep that loses its session still calls every operation, but the requests die at the auth middleware and never reach a handler. Measured from schemathesis-metrics.jsonl. Caught 240/309 operations stuck at 401.
LiveRun validity (KS-684)declares a run INVALID when errors dominate: more than 10% of operations erroring, or 5+ operations sharing one identical error message. Read from the run’s own JUnit XML, deliberately not from the report’s parsers, so the gate can disagree with the report. Reconstructed against the 2026-08-24 incident (310 of 318 operations = 97.5%) → INVALID.
LiveReport reconciliation (KS-517)the HTML report’s headline numbers must equal Schemathesis’ own console summary. Enforces the three-way parity MUST: console = results.json = HTML report. Fails closed — a missing artefact is “cannot verify”, never a pass. Caveat: run.py evaluates it (and the baseline gate) only when every earlier gate passed, so it is skipped on any sweep that found failures — open as KS-752. Until that lands, run it by hand on such a run.
LiveSweep outcome (KS-1408)Schemathesis 4.29.0 made exit 2 mean “nothing tested, or a schema / config / internal error” and 130 mean “interrupted”. src/sweep_outcome.py classifies the exit code once — PASSED (0), FAILED (1), INVALID (2), TIMED OUT (124, the harness’s own kill), INTERRUPTED (130), UNKNOWN (anything else) — and the console Status: line, results.json and the Verdict section’s Outcome row all render that one value. Previously every non-zero code was recorded as failed, and at 4.28.0 a sweep that tested nothing exited 0. Only PASSED is green.
LiveClosing banner (KS-571)the banner at the end of a run now counts every gate that feeds the exit code (run validity, NDJSON completeness, report reconciliation, triaged baseline, IDOR, integration, anchoring, preconditions, auth coverage) and names a gated suite that was skipped, with its reason, instead of printing OVERALL: PASSED over a failing exit code. This reverses KS-684's narrower banner (sweep and IDOR only).
LiveKnown tool false-positive class, kept visible (KS-1414)from Schemathesis 4.29.x a negative case can have its mutated body overwritten by a pool-drawn valid value, so the platform rightly accepts a VALID request and negative_data_rejection still reports “Invalid data should have been rejected” (55–95 per full sweep). A report section, a console block and a results.json block count them; nothing is filtered or baselined, and it is informational, not a gate. Since 2026-10-07 the same rule covers by_design_input_tolerance_guard: a request valid as sent (a drawn-over body, or a path whose values are each drawn or valid) no longer fails the guard, and the section counts the guard’s failures and its valid-as-sent passes. Of the guard’s 12 failures on the KS-1439 sweeps, 6 were valid as sent and 6 genuine (audit-log limit=201, KS-1359).
LiveOne run is one draw — seed + --repeat N (KS-1680)a failure appears only when the run's random seed draws the case that reaches it, and sometimes only when another operation in the same sweep created its data: three pr runs on one build found 11 / 9 / 8 failures. Every run now states its seed and whether it was fixed on the console, in results.json and in the Overview. run.py <tier> --repeat N runs the tier N times (each a complete normal run) and counts each pair as k/N — N/N deterministic, k/N seed-dependent — then sweeps every failing operation alone on the same seeds: a pair that never fails alone is flagged needs other operations' data; an isolated sweep that tested nothing is inconclusive, never a pass. The baseline gate over a set fails an untriaged pair seen in any run, and --compare calls a pair fixed only at N/N → 0/N on a check that inspects the response and when the later set reached the status it failed on (otherwise not reached; a check that fails on its status reads gone (not proven fixed)). The single-run Delta tab now compares only with an earlier run of the same profile (a first pre-merge was once diffed against a pr run: 69 bogus “regressions”).
LiveFresh-clone preconditions (KS-955)a fresh clone used to fail every suite at login in a way that read as a product regression: unseeded personas 401'd (a 100% k6 error rate, an INVALID sweep), the failed logins tripped the F-06 lockout, and with no GATEWAY_VOUCH_SECRET the cross-tenant tests reported “BUG-ISOLATION-001 regression” (KS-1704). Each suite now logs its personas in once before it sends anything — Schemathesis run.py, Akto's personaLoginSetup, k6's runner, Playwright's auth-setup — and stops with KS-955 precondition: and the causes in order (not seeded, locked out, wrong password). The two cross-tenant tests use gateway_vouch_active: it sets a random per-run vouch secret on a local stack the user owns and restores it, or fails with the precondition, never the regression wording. bootstrap-env.sh now generates the secret for a fresh clone, and the lockout reset is in systemTest/CLAUDE.md.
The same blind spot in Akto — a template that was selected but never ran (KS-710 · KS-717)
Akto’s version of “a check that never ran cannot fail”. The test-id catalog is generated from the template files, and check-test-ids diffs that render against the committed catalog — both sides file-derived, so it is structurally incapable of noticing that Akto never loaded a template. A selected-but-absent id produces no testing_run_result document at all, and Akto reports vulnerable 0 exactly as it does for a template that ran and found nothing. Measured on the full OWASP run, 2026-08-28, Akto 2.22.2: 207 ids selected, 193 exercised, verdict PASS. Re-measured on slot 2, 2026-09-28, Akto 2.35.6 (KS-1286): 194 templates initiated, 50,018 result docs across 347 endpoints — the regenerated catalog is byte-identical to 2.22.2’s, and 207→194 is KS-717 dropping ids Akto could never execute rather than lost coverage.
StatusGate / checkWhat it does
LiveCatalog vs loaded library (KS-717)a live assertion in SECUURA_STACK_SLOT=1 npm run test:setup reads yaml_templates straight from Mongo (src/setup/loadedTemplates.ts, slot-aware via AKTO_PREFIX) and diffs it against the catalog in both directions, failing on drift either way. Accepted differences are ticketed entries in KNOWN_CATALOG_DRIFT, and the test also fails when a listed entry stops drifting — an exemption cannot outlive its reason.
LiveExcluded from the catalogan id Akto can never execute must not be selected. 8 Threat-Protection rules carry no execute: block (KS-710); 5 carry upstream’s inactive: true, which Akto stores but its engine skips via fetchOnlyActive (KS-717 §3). 1 more (BYPASS_CAPTCHA_REMOVING_COOKIE) Akto refuses to store, because its info.references: is empty and Jackson cannot coerce that to a list. Catalog 207 → 199 → 194 ids.
LiveReported, never silentload-templates names every file Akto rejected and Akto’s own actionErrors; generate-test-ids reports exclusions and, separately, files with a YAML defect Akto tolerates and we now tolerate too (which ARE catalogued — LFI_IN_HEADERS_LINUX had never executed once). The HTML report renders exercised / selected with the shortfall named, not a bare count.
Outcome taxonomy — five categories, shared across all three surfaces
The taxonomy is closed and shared: a category exists in the console, in results.json and in the HTML report, with the same label and the same count, or it is a design error. results.json is the source of truth; the other two are renderings of it. Each run also writes Schemathesis's native HTML report at <run>/schemathesis-native-html/index.html (linked from the harness report; KS-1615).
PASS — exercised, no violation
FAIL — exercised, violated a check
UNVERIFIED — should have run, did not; gates the run (KS-478)
OUT OF SCOPE — excluded by mode, not by accident (KS-519)
SKIPPED — a precondition was never met (KS-684)
SKIPPED is new in KS-684. Previously the banner rendered a strict PASSED/FAILED binary, so API_TOKEN not found turned four healthy suites — GDPR IDOR (KS-258), live integration (KS-416), anchoring integrity (KS-489-D) and state-machine preconditions (KS-478) — into FAILED on the 2026-08-24 run, sending readers after defects that did not exist.
An unmet precondition is not a test result.
A SKIPPED suite now contributes neither a pass nor a failure to OVERALL, and each row carries its reason — the two skip causes (“no credentials configured” vs “the platform did not answer”) stay distinguishable because they need different remedies.
Counting a skip as a pass would be the opposite and worse error.

Note on "Separate KS Instance": under the consolidated build-once/fan-out topology each suite job boots its own fully-isolated stack — unique COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME/STACK_PREFIX and a per-suite host-port offset, with each tool pointed at its own gateway (each an isolated stack; the CI-only per-suite port numbers are historical and are not slot ports).
Isolation then came from both the per-suite ports and GitHub-hosted runners being single-tenant/ephemeral (one stack per runner), not from a shared default port.
Locally, isolation is the stack slot and every port is the slot-1 base + 100·(N−1).

8. Local Stack Slots — Running Four Configurations at Once (KS-666)

8a. A LOCAL run must name its slot (KS-1016, 2026-09-11)
Every harness — Schemathesis, k6, Playwright, Akto and the shared provisioning step — refuses to start against a local target (localhost, 127.0.0.1, [::1], host.docker.internal) when neither SECUURA_STACK_SLOT nor the platform-s alias STACK_SLOT is set, and prints the command to run instead: 
No stack slot named. Every LOCAL system-test run must say which Docker stack it targets
(target: http://localhost:6882/api). Name the slot and run again, for example:
  SECUURA_STACK_SLOT=<n> python3 scripts/run.py pr
  or: systemTest/run-in-slot.sh <n> python3 scripts/run.py pr
Remote targets need no slot; CI (CI=true) is exempt.
Local only. A remote target carries no slot and is left alone; CI is exempt because its isolated per-suite stacks are local by construction and deliberately unslotted (CI=true).
Before this rule an unset slot meant slot 1 silently — another ticket's stack on a shared machine.
Proven on slot 2: no slot → exit 2, 0 docker calls, nothing provisioned; STACK_SLOT=2 → 1,759 requests to the slot-2 gateway (6882 + 100·(2−1)).

Four slots per platform, and the numbering is shared with platform-s (PS-622). Every published port is the historic one plus 100 × (N − 1), so platform-s slot N and platform-k slot N pair up with no configuration: platform-k slot N's gateway lands on 6882 + 100 × (N − 1). platform-s exports STACK_SLOT; platform-k reads SECUURA_STACK_SLOT and falls back to it, so a single export in a worktree drives both platforms.
Four is a deliberate ceiling — the two platforms first collide at platform-s slot 9, where its PMA proxy (8081) meets platform-k tokenomics (8881).
⚠ The same four ports mean different things locally and in CI. Section 5 (historical, Actions retired 2026-08-27) gave each suite — schemathesis, playwright, performance, akto — its own CI-only port block because each CI job booted its own single-tenant stack on an ephemeral runner.
Locally the ports are per stack slot (slot-1 base + 100·(N−1)), and every suite targets whichever slot it was pointed at.
Reading a local port as a CI suite (or the reverse) will attribute a result to the wrong thing.
Every harness follows the slot, and every result names it. Source systemTest/slot-target.sh and Schemathesis (SECUURA_BASE_URL), Playwright (GATEWAY_URL), Akto (SECUURA_API_URL, plus its own side-stack, mongo volume and dashboard port) and the performance runner (PERF_BASE_URL) all aim at the same stack.
Akto and the performance runner used to default to localhost:6882 on their own, so a run silently tested slot 1 whichever slot was meant; since KS-1386 an unslotted local run is refused instead — there is no default URL. Playwright is the exception since KS-682: config/stackSlot.ts reads SECUURA_STACK_SLOT itself, derives the gateway, refuses a malformed or out-of-range slot and a label naming another slot, writes results/playwright-report-<ticket>-<ts>-slot<N> behind a results/latest-slot<N> pointer, and serves the report on 9324 + 100·(N−1).
Pinned by the unit suite in systemTest/playwright/tests-unit/ (292 cases on the Mac, 2026-09-10; 389 passing in 6.5 s, Mac, 2026-10-06) — including a boundary suite: an explicit slot outside 1–4 derives no port, a suffix that spells the slot any way but the wrapper's (-slot01) is refused, and a pinned report port must be decimal digits; KS-1056 tracks the other three.
A fresh local stack needs its bootstrap admin, or every harness degrades. Actor provisioning (fixtures/provision-actors.ts) grants roles as admin@secuura.com; that account is seeded only when the auth service receives ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD at build time. docker-compose.yml forwards it since 2026-09-10 (KS-682, from KS-971) — before that the templated value never reached the container, the account was never seeded, and provisioning collapsed every actor to OWNER and refused the manifest (KS-969, KS-972). check-stack-safety.sh now holds the forward as an invariant.
Since 2026-09-10 Playwright's global-setup also passes its slot-derived gateway to provisioning (--base-url): an unsourced SECUURA_STACK_SLOT=N run provisions on slot N rather than on slot 1, which it did before — found on the slot-2 rotation, invisible on slot 1.
A superseded manifest keeps its slot segment (actors-slot<N>.superseded-<ts>.json) — found on the slot-4 rotation.
Schemathesis resolves its own slot (KS-1016). It no longer depends on that export: src/slot.py reads SECUURA_STACK_SLOT (or platform-s's STACK_SLOT) and derives the gateway by the same historic + 100 × (N − 1) rule, so SECUURA_STACK_SLOT=<n> alone targets :6882 + 100·(n−1).
It is one resolver for the runner, the hooks and the persona logins.
Those three used to answer differently — constants.py preferred API_BASE_URL, cli.py preferred SECUURA_BASE_URL, and config/settings.py and config/fixtures.py ignored API_BASE_URL entirely — so a shell carrying only one of the pair drove the runner to one slot and every login to another, within a single run, with nothing reporting it.
The checked-in [tool.schemathesis] base-url in pyproject.toml is gone for the same reason: a file in git cannot know which slot a run is aimed at, and a direct st run consulted nothing else.
The resolver's edges are pinned in tests/unit/test_slot_resolver_edges.py: padding around the slot, a trailing slash or a missing /api on either base-URL variable, a blank-but-present SECUURA_BASE_URL, and — found by probing after the four-slot live series — a whitespace SECUURA_STACK_SLOT that used to mask a valid STACK_SLOT and default the run to slot 1.
Four further modules close the branches around the fix: test_stack_postgres_fixture.py (the fixture the migrated call site runs through: skip, cross-slot refusal, the guard actually called), test_compose_project_resolution.py (which compose project a recreate is aimed at: slot-prefixed probe order, blank label, fallback, explicit override), test_slot_rule_executes_like_the_shell.py (sources stack_env.sh per slot and compares what it exports, so the pin is on behaviour rather than text), test_observability_best_effort.py (a refused Pushgateway or Grafana degrades to False, never to a red run); and the no-hardcoded-slot guard now walks src/, scripts/ and config/ as well as tests/.
The resolver refuses what stack_env.sh refuses — 0, 01, abc, 5 — and test_slot_rule_executes_like_the_shell.py sources the shell per slot to prove both sides agree on behaviour, not text.
Proven by rotation, one slot at a time (KS-1016, 2026-09-10/11). Slots 4 → 3 → 2 → 1, each built from an empty host with every other slot torn down, launched with no slot-targeting variable set and every docker call audited: every request to the slot's own gateway, zero to any other, zero docker calls, artifacts and latest-slotN carrying the slot.
On 2026-09-11, with develop forwarding ADMIN_USER_PASSWORD, the first valid sweeps ran (0 of 316 operations errored) and the four harnesses ran in series on slot 4 — Schemathesis pr, k6 smoke, Playwright ci:e2e, Akto pre-merge — with slots 1–3 empty throughout. Rule from that series: export BOOTSTRAP_ADMIN_PASSWORD on every suite run, Schemathesis included. The first provisioning on a fresh stack creates the generated actors; without the variable they are created as OWNER and every later harness — k6, Playwright, Akto — inherits them (DEGRADED, and Playwright 400s at auth-setup) until the slot's database is reset. Since KS-1016 provisioning refuses instead (assertBootstrapAvailable in fixtures/provision-actors.ts, unit-tested in performance/tests/unit/fixtures/): an unavailable bootstrap admin throws before the first registration, so nothing is created and the next run with the variable set provisions correctly.
And every slot reader — the shared writer, Playwright, k6, Akto, Schemathesis's manifest reader and src/slot.py — honours platform-s's STACK_SLOT alias in stack_env.sh:37's order (SECUURA_STACK_SLOT wins, blank falls through, a malformed alias is refused), pinned per harness and by __tests__/manifest_readers_agree.test.sh.
DEGRADED reports what it did to the manifest, strict arm included (KS-981, 2026-09-29). When provisioning fails, the pre-suite moves any manifest on disk aside so no harness reads stale actors — with or without SYSTEMTEST_REQUIRE_PROVISIONED.
The strict banner used to print only FATAL, so a manifest that could not be moved, and is still on disk for the next run on that slot, went unreported.
Both arms now print moved-to / none-on-disk / could-not-move, the last naming the file consumers read (actors-slotN.json, not the pre-KS-971 actors.json).
Pinned by __tests__/quarantine_call_sites.test.sh: 5 cells red on the previous code, 17 of 17 green after.
A failed login now says which cause, and a refused connection names its port (KS-1167, 2026-09-14). The shared pre-suite login dropped the HTTP status, so bootstrap admin: UNAVAILABLE explained every non-200 as “check the password” — a 429 from the per-IP login limiter included, on the first step every harness runs. fixtures/login-outcome.ts classifies the attempt (unreachable > rate-limited > rejected > unexpected) and each branch names a different next step; the fetch in fixtures/provision.ts was unguarded, so a refused connection reached the DEGRADED banner as the bare fetch failed with the ECONNREFUSED <host>:<port> lost in an empty-message AggregateError; fixtures/describe-error.ts now renders it.
Playwright's auth-setup diagnoses its own login the same way (limiter / EMPTY password from a withheld manifest / rejected / unhealthy) and its global-setup refuses on a 429 ping rather than proceeding into provisioning inside a cooldown.
Proven red→green against a stub gateway answering one fixed status and a port proven closed (__tests__/bootstrap_login_diagnosis.test.sh: 10 of 16 cells red on the previous fixtures), with no stack.
The API Explorer resolves its stack slot too (KS-1386, 2026-09-29). It was the last systemTest package fixed to slot 1: an explorer generated while working on slot N offered slot 1's gateway as its Local server and printed slot 1's health-check curls, and a server chosen on one slot's page was reused by another's (every explorer opened from disk shares one browser-storage origin).
Generation now takes SECUURA_STACK_SLOT (or STACK_SLOT) and refuses a generation that names neither — under CI too, since it has no URL of its own — and the page ignores a stored server it does not offer.
Pinned by per-slot unit tests derived from slot 1, a parity test against fixtures/slot.ts, and a guard that keeps slot 1's port out of every other file under api-explorer/src/.
Nothing defaults to slot 1 any more, in any harness (KS-1386, 2026-09-29). Five slot resolvers turned an unnamed slot into slot 1, so an unslotted run could provision, log in, scan or stop containers on slot 1 while the rest of it was aimed elsewhere — Schemathesis's setup minted an admin API key there, Akto checked its scan target but not its own dashboard, and prove-slot-isolation.sh defaulted its victim slot to 3.
Every stack-touching entry point now refuses a local run that names no slot; CI and remote targets stay exempt from naming one, but with no slot and no URL every harness refuses; an exempt run is labelled unslotted, never slot1.
No slot 2–4 value is typed anywhere: tests derive them from slot 1, and __tests__/no_hardcoded_slot_literals.test.sh scans every harness. One bounded exemption (KS-1450): the Schemathesis baseline's $generated.from_runs run ids record which sweep produced a row and cannot carry an inline marker, so a lone string element of that exact shape is exempt in that one file — and a guard cell asserts every exempted line really is a from_runs member, so the exemption cannot widen silently.
Same branch: the Akto offline gate no longer spawns docker, no script prints part of the API token, api-explorer's golden snapshot is tracked, the Schemathesis offline suites fail any test that writes into the real output/reports/, and the Akto and Performance no-slot refusals name the npm script that was run. slot-target.sh (KS-1389) and observability/ (KS-1388) are tracked separately.
The slot gate is driven as a process, and the offline unit suites are slot-independent (KS-1167). Playwright and k6 proved the KS-1016 guard was called by reading the runner as text; both now spawn the real entry point with the slot family stripped and read the exit code — and npm run report (Playwright), which resolved slot 1 silently, consults the rule (SECUURA_STACK_SLOT=1 npm run report).
Measured the same day: the Playwright unit suite was 348/348 from an unslotted shell and 345–347/348 from a slotted one; Performance 1077/1077 versus 1060–1067.
The suites' verdicts depended on which worktree ran them — files cleared the slot family only in afterEach, never the STACK_SLOT alias, and k6's runner modules freeze their slot at import.
Both now strip the slot family before every file (Playwright: clear-before-each plus a childEnv() door for spawns; Performance: a vitest setupFiles entry), and each carries a matrix that re-runs the suite under no slot and slots 1–4 — both variables and the wrapper's suffix shape — demanding identical counts.
371/371 and 1083/1083 under every shape after the fix.
The push-time format gate no longer passes having checked nothing (KS-1063, 2026-09-29). For a systemTest-only push the hook skips the platform preflight by design, so systemTest/scripts/check-package-format.sh is the one gate that runs.
It skips a package whose deps are not installed, and when it skipped every package it touched it exited 0 on 0 package(s) checked, N skipped, 0 failed — the same observable as a clean check.
It now refuses with NOTHING CHECKED and says it is not a formatting failure; a run that checked at least one package still passes.
Pinned by __tests__/package_format_gate.test.sh (4 cells red before, 33 of 33 after).
⚠ A cross-slot read is refused, not merely improbable (KS-1016). The anchoring DB sweeps and the compose controller both compare the container's slot with the target gateway's slot and stop if they differ, naming both sides.
Before this, test_anchor_read_honesty ran docker exec secuura-postgres with the name hardcoded — slot 1's container and only slot 1's — so a slot-3 run created a document on slot 3 and then counted contradictory rows in slot 1's anchor_store.
Nothing refused the connection, because every slot ships the same Postgres password (KS-731), so the answer came back and read as authoritative.
The compose path had no guard at all and is the more dangerous of the two: it stops and recreates containers, so an unsourced shell would have taken another ticket's stack down while asserting against this one.
An unidentifiable slot on either side — the isolated CI stack, a demo target — is allowed through; only two known, differing slots are refused.
Run metrics are grouped per slot (KS-1016). The Pushgateway key is /job/integration/environment/<env>/slot/<N>.
There is a single shared secuura-obs-pushgateway on host :9099, so the URL cannot be per-slot; and a push to an existing key replaces that group.
Two concurrent slots therefore overwrote each other's run summary, both reported success, and the surviving series described whichever slot pushed last.
Slot isolation covered the stack under test but not the record of what was tested.
Result isolation is a MUST, with no exception. Folders and files both carry the Linear ticket and the slot — results-ks-666-slot<n>.json, output/reports-slot<n>/pr-ks-666-<ts>, test-fast-ks-666-<ts>-slot<n>.
Slot 1 is labelled too: an unlabelled results-ks-666.json was the one set nobody could relate back to a slot or port.
Three of the four harnesses name runs by the second, so two slots finishing together resolved to a single path — measured on this Mac 2026-08-20, where concurrent Playwright runs on slots 1 and 3 shared the start time 10:55:12.567Z, and Schemathesis and Akto both produced identical timestamps.
The latest pointer is slot-scoped for the same reason.
⚠ Within a slot, suites run in SERIES. Slots run in parallel with each other; suites within one slot do not.
The reason is the platform's per-IP login rate limiter, not resource contention — every harness authenticates through the same gateway as the same personas, and from the stack's point of view every local suite shares one IP. All four harnesses are affected — Akto, Schemathesis, Playwright and the performance suite alike.
Any can trip the limiter and any can be starved by another; Schemathesis is simply where it was first seen, because its report names the cause, while the others surface it as login failures, empty result sets or timeouts that read as product bugs. Once rate limiting appears, wait 15 minutes before starting any further tests — the window has to drain, and restarting inside it both wastes the run and pushes the window out.
Measured 2026-08-20 running Playwright, Schemathesis and k6 together against slot 1: Schemathesis logged 300 engine errors across 289 operations, every one login for persona=super_admin is rate-limited.
That failure lies twice, which is why it is worth naming here. The report was headed PASSED — the operations were never exercised, so nothing could fail — and the errors are filed as engine errors, reading as a Schemathesis fault rather than the platform's limiter doing its job. Use systemTest/run-in-slot.sh <slot> <command>, which holds an exclusive per-slot lock. LOCAL_LOGIN_LIMITER_DISABLED=true (KS-191) suppresses the limiter, but only if the stack was started with it, and it changes the system under test.
Measured on this Mac, 2026-08-20. Four platform-k stacks (33 containers each, 132 total) plus a platform-s stack ran together in 7.2 GiB of a 31.3 GiB Docker Desktop allocation (recorded as 6 CPU then; docker info reports 8 CPU / 31.3 GiB on 2026-10-06), with all 31 bound ports attributable to a platform and slot and no collision. Memory is not the constraint; CPU is — load averaged ~23 with four stacks idle, so four concurrent suites is a different question and has not been measured.

Slot isolation used to be opt-in, and forgetting was silent (KS-687). Every slot-carrying value the Akto harness used arrived from slot-target.sh; the package itself read SECUURA_STACK_SLOT in one place, to word an error.
Correctness was a property of the operator.
It is now a property of the code: validate() refuses a run whose pieces name different slots, an unusable slot request (5, abc, 3.5 — never defaulted to slot 1, matching stack_env.sh), and an artefact suffix that is a path; pre-flight derives its probe from the same function the scan uses, so it cannot vouch for a neighbour (the first live slot-4 run passed pre-flight on host.docker.internal:<slot-4 gateway> while the scan went to localhost:<slot-4 gateway> inside the container (6882 + 100·(4−1)) — 8,816 connectivity skips under a PASS in 25 s); and after every scan the persisted artefact is walked and any local URL on another slot's port fails the run.
Proven live on all four slots on 2026-09-10 — 8,902–8,933 executed, 0 vulnerable, 2,619–2,635 references to the slot's own gateway, zero to any other — and again on slot 4 from the develop-merged tree on 2026-09-11 (9,105 / 9,138 executed, zero foreign); the leak check names the foreign hosts the moment the same artefact is claimed for a different slot.
And the gate that could not see the original defect now can (KS-687 F2).check-akto-container-names.sh scans src/ bin/ scripts/ for *.ts *.sh *.mjs, matches a slot-1 container name as a literal or as a defaulted variable (${VAR:-akto-mongo}, ?? 'akto-testing'), and its non-vacuity assert names the directories the corpus must contribute rather than counting files — the count passed over the directory F1 lived in.
Red-first: F1's original line is the first fixture.

9. Auth surface — connector tokens on the users routes (KS-564, KS-1402)

9a. KS-1402 — GET /api/users/lookup accepts a connector token (Kam ruling 2026-10-02, option (a))
What it pins. Platform S authenticates with an sk_ connector key, so its token is a type: 'connector' token rather than an interactive access token.
Before KS-1402 only POST /api/users/stub accepted one (KS-564, Option A); GET /api/users/lookup still used plain authenticate(), so every Platform-S transfer-custody call 401'd and fell back.
Both routes now go through authenticateAccessOrConnector(). The token type is not the permission. The route's own role/scope gate still runs afterwards, so users:read is the effective gate on /lookup, and a cross-tenant lookup still returns 404 — not 200-empty, so positive existence is not readable from the response shape.
The audit label is route-neutral, deliberately. The connector-accepted log line read users/stub: … unconditionally, so once a second route accepted connector tokens every /lookup call would have written an audit line naming a route it never touched.
It now carries route: req.baseUrl + req.path. req.originalUrl was rejected for this field because it carries the query string: measured on GET /api/users/lookup?email=alice%40example.com, req.originalUrl is /api/users/lookup?email=alice%40example.com while req.baseUrl + req.path is /api/users/lookup — so originalUrl would put the email address in the clear in the audit log, which is the very thing maskEmail() exists to prevent.
9b. The suite cells, and how to run them
File: Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/__tests__/ks1402-lookup-accepts-connector-token.test.ts — 183 lines, four cells, each minting a real type: 'connector' token via generateConnectorToken. The authenticator is never mocked (0 mocks of ../middleware/authenticate, against a must-hit control of 9 vi.mock calls elsewhere in the same file), because a mocked authenticator cannot observe the thing the ticket is about. 
# Run it (services/auth). NOTE: `npm test` here is WATCH mode — use the explicit run form.
cd Blockchain/Dev/services/auth
npx vitest run                                                       # the whole suite
npx vitest run src/__tests__/ks1402-lookup-accepts-connector-token.test.ts   # just these cells

CELL 1  a connector token carrying users:read REACHES the handler          200
CELL 2  a connector token WITHOUT users:read is refused 403, not 401       403
CELL 3  an interactive ACCESS token still works                            200   <- the CONTROL
CELL 4  a tenant-A connector token cannot read a tenant-B-only email       404
Red-first / green-after, measured 2026-10-04. With the new test against base product code: cells 1, 2 and 4 red (expected 401 to be 200, … to be 403, … to be 404) and cell 3 green.
Cell 3 is the control that makes those three flips a statement about the product rather than about the harness.
At the PR head: 4/4 green.
Suite totals moved 77 → 78 files and 836 → 840 tests, both sides measured on the same base.
Timing — and what is deliberately NOT changed here. 10. API contract — the delegation GET spec declares its own envelope (KS-1015)

10a. KS-1015 — GET /api/delegations/{id} publishes the envelope its handler returns
What it pins. The published contract for GET /api/delegations/{id} declared a bare Delegation record as its 200 body, while the handler (routes/delegations.ts, GET /:id) answers { success, data: { delegation, chain } } — the chain being whatever buildDelegationChain() returns.
Schemathesis flagged the 200 as response_schema_conformance in the sweep of 2026-09-29. The spec now follows the runtime, not the other way round: the 200 content is a successEnvelope(...) whose data carries the unchanged Delegation component by $ref alongside the chain object. invalidReason is declared optional because the chain only carries it when isValid is false.
It NARROWS KS-1015, it does not close it. The ticket is a sweep finding covering 28 check/operation pairs with no live owner; this change owns one of them.
The remaining pairs stay open on the ticket.

11. RFC 3161 Timestamp Token Verification (KS-1404)

What changed.services/timestamping accepted an unsigned timestamp token as valid.
The old verifyRealToken walked the ASN.1 tree and returned valid: true whenever any OCTET STRING equalled the expected document digest — no signature check, no certificate chain, no TSTInfo parse, no algorithm-OID check.
A second path accepted a JSON {"hash":"…"} token outright.
Both are closed.

11.1 The verification chain, in order

KS-1404 ITEM 2 (Seat D 5th): the verifier binds the signer certificate via signingCertificate(V2) and builds the chain from the token's own certificates to a pinned root.
The signer is selected by an exact SignerIdentifier match — issuer+serial or subjectKeyIdentifier — and the previous ?? certs[0] fallback is gone, so a token whose SignerInfo names nothing it carries is refused rather than checked against whichever certificate happened to be first.
The token's other certificates are passed to the chain engine as untrusted intermediates; trustedCerts remains the configured anchors alone, so carrying an intermediate can never create trust. rsaEncryption (digest taken from digestAlgorithm) and RSASSA-PSS (parameters parsed, never defaulted) are accepted, because those are the algorithms the pinned providers measurably use.
A defect of this PR, found and fixed inside it, and the cell that caught it. The first version of the chain fix passed certs: [signer, ...intermediates]. pkijs treats the LAST element of certs as the end-entity — its own documented example is certs: [rootCa, intermediateCa, leafCert] — so an intermediate was validated as the leaf, and a token whose signer chained to nothing was ACCEPTED whenever some certificate it carried chained to an anchor.
The order is now [...intermediates, signer]. CHAIN-3 is the only cell that fails on the reversed order, and it stays in the suite for that reason.
Strict DERdefinite, minimal lengths, nothing trailing.
BER indefinite-length encoding is refused: a genuine token re-wrapped as 30 80 … 00 00 was accepted before this change.
ContentInfo is id-signedData; SignedData's eContentType is id-ct-TSTInfo.
TSTInfo is parsed, and the message imprint is read from messageImprint.hashedMessage — never searched for in the tree.
Exactly one SignerInfo, whose signed attributes carry contentType = id-ct-TSTInfo and messageDigest = digest(eContent).
The signature over the signed attributes re-encoded as SET OF, against the signer certificate's public key.
The signer certificate carries EKU id-kp-timeStamping, is valid at genTime, and chains to a configured trust anchor.

11.2 Fail-closed, and what that means operationally

Trust anchors come from TSA_TRUST_ANCHORS_PEM (PEM text, or a path to a bundle), committed as config. Unset or empty means every real DER token verifies false with reason no trust anchor configured. Stored tokens continue to verify through the database-row branch (same hash and byte-identical proof), which this change does not touch. Compose and per-environment wiring landed in KS-1404's second half and is described in 11.4; this sentence previously read “Compose and per-environment wiring is a separate step, so which environments have an anchor in effect is not covered here”, which was true of #1376 and is now false.

11.4 Compose and per-environment wiring (KS-1404, Seat D 8th)

#1376 closed the forgeable paths in the verifier and committed the roots, but nothing delivered an anchor to a running service, so every real DER token was refused on every box with no trust anchor configured — regardless of what the TSA did.
Two changes close that, and one measurement decides their shape.
Item Value
Measured per environment, read-only, 2026-10-05 On both live boxes: TSA_URL PRESENT but EMPTY, TSA_TRUST_ANCHORS_PEM ABSENT, /app/config absent from the image. An empty TSA_URL is not “no provider”: it falls through to the code default, and /health read from inside each container reports D-Trust GmbH, https://timestamp.d-trust.net/tsa, eidasQualified: true. Neither box runs docker-compose.production.yml.
Change 1 — compose The timestamping environment: list passes TSA_TRUST_ANCHORS_PEM, defaulting to /app/config/tsa-trust-anchors-dtrust.crt. The default is what makes the anchor effective with no .env edit on any box; a box .env can still override it. Measured: no box-level TSA override exists on either host to fight it.
Change 2 — the image The Dockerfile's runtime stage copies config/ to /app/config, before the chmod -R a+rX. Order is load-bearing: the service runs as the unprivileged nodejs user, so a file copied after the chmod ships unreadable. Before this, the runtime stage copied only /app/dist.
Scope — ONE provider's root config/tsa-trust-anchors-dtrust.crt holds D-TRUST Root CA 1 2017 alone, byte-identical to block 1 of the committed two-root bundle (2,354 bytes; DER SHA-256 4d24807b…aef6, matching config/README.md). Nothing was fetched and no new root is introduced. Kam's card secuura-ks1404-tsa-trust-and-library-1004 = a pins “that provider's published root”, and since both boxes resolve to D-Trust, the DigiCert root is needed by neither.

C2, D and E are CONTROLS that pass at base AND head and are stated as such, not counted as red: C2 that an anchor delivered as a file path is read and used while unset fails closed, D that an untrusted-root DER token is still refused, E that a mock JSON token is still refused.
Why C2 exists The pre-existing KS-1404 suite passes the anchor as inline PEM text everywhere. The readFileSync branch of readTrustAnchorsPem() — the one the compose default makes every box use — had no coverage at all. This wiring depends entirely on it.

12. GET /api/anchors/:id reports blockNumber as a number (KS-1333)

What this pins.services/originate/src/services/anchorStateSync.ts has four writers that persist blockHeight: anchor.blockNumber || 0 without shaping the value, and anchor.blockNumber arrives from GET /api/anchors/:id.
KS-1333's first step is to measure whether that route can hand them a raw pg int8 string.
Measured at source: it cannot. rowToAnchor converts block_number through Number() (services/anchoring/src/index.ts:1317), and the handler answers the mapped anchor.blockNumber || null rather than the raw row.
So the route answers a number or null, and the ticket's own rule applies — a recorded reason and a cell pinning it, not a coercion. This block is that cell.

12.1 The cells, and why the guard is source-text

Three cells in services/anchoring/src/__tests__/ks1333-get-by-id-blocknumber-is-a-number.test.ts. index.ts calls app.listen at import, so no test imports it; the guard therefore reads index.ts as text over the two lines that make the answer a number. B1 pins the Number() conversion in rowToAnchor. C1 pins that the handler answers the mapped value and never row.block_number. C2 pins that the by-id lookup maps its row through rowToAnchor at all — without C2, B1 could pass while the handler read a different row path entirely.

15. /revoke is one atomic transition (KS-1278)

What this pins.POST /api/documents/:id/revoke decided “already revoked” on a READ (routes/documents.ts:2374) and then ran an unconditional UPDATE.
Two overlapping revokes could both pass that read, so both answered 200, both wrote an action_provenance row and both emitted an anchor call.
The decision now lives IN the UPDATE: updateDocument takes an ifStatusIsNot option that adds AND (${guardStatus}::text IS NULL OR status IS DISTINCT FROM ${guardStatus}::text) to the WHERE, and a guarded write that changed no row returns null.
The loser of the race answers the same 400 BAD_REQUEST “Document is already revoked” as a sequential caller, and returns before recordOnBehalfOf — so it records no provenance row and emits no anchor.
Scope. This completes the ticket’s scope — the atomic transition, the 400 for the loser, and provenance and anchor only for the winner.
The PR says Refs KS-1278, not Closes. The row-lock alternative is not taken.
What a null from the guarded write means, and what each meaning is pinned by.updateDocument already returned null for a missing document (documentRepo.ts:543 at 4a1620588819; :538 at the branch base 32e058975d4e), so null is not a single condition and the route must not read it as one.
On the guarded path it can arise three ways:
A genuine raceanother revoke changed the row between this request's read and its write.
The write refuses in the UPDATE, so exactly one of two overlapping writers wins. Instrument: cell R1, which also asserts 0 anchor emissions on the losing path, not only 0 provenance rows.
The guard itself is pinned by cell R2, which asserts the guard clause by exact text and the guard’s own two parameters by position — a weaker assertion on either half is satisfied by a vacuous guard, or by the SET clause’s new status standing in for the guard value.
The row was deleted inside the windowthe answer is 400 where 404 belongs.
This is unchanged by round 2 and is tracked as KS 1419. Instrument: none live — unmeasured against a real database.
A revoke addressed by the platform UUIDfixed in round 2. Both reads fall back to the primary key for a UUID-shaped id (documentRepo.ts:244-251) and the API hands clients that key as documentUuid (:172), but the guarded UPDATE keyed on external_id. At the branch base and at round 1 a sequential, non-race revoke of a live, owned, unrevoked document addressed that way matched 0 rows and answered 400 "Document is already revoked" with 0 provenance rows and the status never written. At round 2 the guarded write keys on the row the read resolved (:616, mirroring the read's own precedence: external_id first, then the primary key), so it answers 200, writes the status and records exactly one provenance row. Instrument: cell N1, red at 4a1620588819 and green at the round-2 head.
The route still 404s at :2367 and 403s at :2371 before the write, so a missing or unowned document never reaches it. Only the opted-in revoke path changed key: the other 12 production updateDocument( callers pass no ifStatusIsNot and take a byte-identical statement (instrument: cell N3).
A non-UUID external id never reaches the ::uuid cast, which would otherwise raise 22P02 (:590; instrument: cell N2, green at both ends).
The remaining residual cases are recorded under Not covered below.

18. OAuth app scopes are a closed vocabulary, and the by-id routes are owner-or-admin (KS-1210)

What this fixes. Any authenticated user, whatever their role, could register an OAuth app — or change another user's app — with any scope list at all, including the wildcard *, the privileged subjects:erase, and strings that are not scopes (made:up).
Both request schemas took z.array(pgSafeStringSchema), i.e. any NUL-free string, and neither POST /apps nor PATCH /apps/:id carried a role or ownership check.
Measured again at this change's base: updateApp(id, updates) and getAppById(id) are keyed on the id ALONE, with no owner predicate — which answers a question KS-1210 itself listed as not measured, and is why the gate belongs in the route handlers rather than the repository.

18.1 Two gates, two lists, and why they are copied rather than imported

Gate 1 closes both schemas to the nine AVAILABLE_SCOPES (services/auth/src/services/oauth.ts:57-67, blob 8995edec6a43): anything else is 400 for every caller, which alone closes the sev-5.
On top of that, the privileged set {admin:read, admin:write} may only be registered by a caller in the four-role platform list — otherwise 403. Gate 2 makes the four by-id routes (GET, PATCH, DELETE, POST .../rotate-secret) answer 404 unless the caller created the app or is in the six-role admin list — 404 rather than 403, so another user's app is not disclosed by the status code.
Neither list is importable: PLATFORM_ADMIN_ROLES is a module-level const that is not exported (routes/users.ts:192) and ADMIN_ROLES is local to that file's GET '/' handler (routes/users.ts:439), both blob ea9f8da97a04.
They are therefore copied into routes/oauth.ts by name, with a drift cell that reads users.ts as source and fails if either copy stops matching — so the duplication cannot rot silently.
An export edit in users.ts was deliberately not made: that file belongs to other rows this round.

19. change-password reads the hash it verifies (KS-1005)

What changed.POST /api/users/me/change-password answered 404 for every password account. services/auth/src/routes/users.ts loaded the row with userRepo.getUserById, whose column list (userRepo.ts USER_COLS, commented “All user columns EXCEPT password_hash”) omits password_hash; the next line throws NotFoundError('User') on !user.passwordHash.
So the hash was always absent and the endpoint was wholly non-functional — not wrong at an edge.
It now calls getUserByIdWithPasswordHash, the hash-carrying variant that already existed and was used once, by mfa.ts, never here. One call site changed; the other seven getUserById call sites in the file are untouched.
The defect was worse than “returns 404”. The throw precedes verifyPassword entirely, so at base the route answered 404 whether the current password was right or wrong — it could not tell the two apart.
Cells A and B pin exactly that asymmetry: A requires 200 for a correct password, B requires 400 for a wrong one.
Both were 404 before the change.

19.1 Why the cells mock the database and not the repository

The defect is the repository’s column list, so a cell that stubbed userRepo.getUserById to hand back a passwordHash would have mocked the defect away and passed on broken code. These cells run the real repository, routes, error handler and argon2/bcrypt password service, and mock only ../db. The mock is faithful on the one property that decides the outcome: it returns password_hash only when the SELECT actually named that column, exactly as Postgres would. Cell C pins the mechanism directly — at base zero SELECTs asked for password_hash.

20. Clearing MFA NULLs the TOTP seed and the hashed backup codes, at all three sites (KS-938)

What this fixes. “MFA disabled” left the TOTP seed and the hashed backup codes in the row.
The flag flipped, the call answered 200 “MFA disabled successfully”, and the credential material survived — so a seed could be re-armed by POST /api/users/me/mfa/verify, which re-arms on the existing user.mfaSecret without minting a new one.
The case that matters is the user who disabled MFA because the authenticator was compromised.

20.1 The mechanism, and the one thing deliberately NOT changed

userRepo.updateUser builds its SET list with if (tsField in updates && updates[tsField] !== undefined). mfa_secret and mfa_backup_codes are in fieldMap, so the map was never the problem — the value guard was. All three clearing sites passed undefined, so a partial UPDATE landed naming only the fields that survived. The undefined skip is NOT changed: every other caller relies on it to mean “leave this column alone”. null passes the guard and writes SQL NULL, and the encryption branch guards on typeof val === 'string', so a null can never enter it. The codebase already knew the rule — wallet.ts carries “null, NOT undefined” for walletAddress (KS 720).

20.2 Three sites, and why the fix is per-site rather than one shared edit

Addressed by symbol, with blobs, because the line numbers move: at this change's base routes/mfa.ts is blob 87d3ee1079fe and routes/users.ts is blob ea9f8da97a04. mfa.ts setup-verify revert (updateUser) and mfa.ts POST /mfa/disable (updateUserOrThrow) each passed undefined for both columns. users.ts POST /me/mfa/disable did not pass mfaBackupCodes at all, so that site needed the key added, not merely re-valued — which is why no single shared edit could have fixed all three.

20.3 Red-first, by assertion

The cells drive the real route handlers over real loopback HTTP with the real userRepo and the real updateUser, stubbing only ../db so the emitted statement can be captured, and they assert the SQL — not the source text, which would still pass if the fix were commented out.
At the base the three site cells fail and the two controls pass (3 failed | 2 passed (5)); at the head 5 passed (5).
Both numbers are non-zero, so the red is a real red and not a load failure.
The base failure quotes the defect verbatim: UPDATE users SET mfa_enabled = $1, verification_level = $2, updated_at = NOW() WHERE id = $3.
The load-bearing control drives the same real updateUser with undefined and requires the two columns to be absent — a cell that cannot tell the fix from its own fallback is not a regression test.

20.4 Residue, named and NOT fixed here

users.ts POST /me/mfa/disable verifies the TOTP only if (user.mfaSecret && ...), so an account with no stored seed disables MFA with no proof of possession at all. That is a separate defect in the same handler and is left for its own ticket rather than widened into this one.

21. An unreadable connector allow-list refuses the create with 503 instead of granting everything (KS-1256)

What this fixes. The connector allow-list is read out of platform settings to decide whether a caller may create a restricted document type.
When that read failed, the parse left connectorConfig = {} — and an empty config reads as no restriction.
So every restricted connector became unrestricted precisely when the platform could not tell what the restrictions were.
This is the same fail-open class KS-1233 closed for the TTL trigger, still open on this path.
The read now fails closed: an unreadable allow-list answers 503 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE and the create is refused until the configuration can be read.

the read THROWS (client MaxRetriesPerRequestError, or JSON.parse on malformed stored bytes) swallowed by a bare } catch {} → no restriction503, create refused
Redis UNAVAILABLEno restriction503, and the read is never performed
Redis available, the settings key ABSENTno restrictionno restriction — deliberately unchanged
the allow-list container is MALFORMED403403, unchanged (KS-1231)
The third row is a decision, not an oversight. It was put to Kam as secuura-connector-allowlist-missing-setting-ks1256-1005 and ruled b, “Keep ‘no restriction’ when unset”, with the detail “No behaviour change; the gap stays for fresh installs.” A fresh install has no platform-settings key, and failing closed there would refuse every connector create on a new deployment.

21.2 Two unreadable paths that do NOT share a mechanism, and why a catch cannot close one of them

Driven against real ioredis 5.11.1 and a real TCP RESP server, not a mock. In the unavailable state getNotificationSettings resolves null without throwing — it reads an empty in-memory store (services/redis.ts:671-678). A catch never observes a resolved null, so the availability test has to come before the read rather than inside the catch. That is why the fix is two edits and not one.
Separately, fallbackMode is set on a sustained runtime outage by retryStrategy at services/redis.ts:78, which carries no NODE_ENV guard. Driven under NODE_ENV=production the branch fires identically, so production reached the fail-open state on a runtime blip despite refusing to START without Redis. The production cell exists to pin that.

21.3 Red-first, by assertion

Six cells, all six green at head. At base, 4 of the 6 are RED — the two CONTROL cells are green at base by design, because they pin behaviour this change does not touch (403 on a malformed container, and a readable allow-list still restricting). A control that reddens with the fix would be testing the fix, not guarding it. Measured by Seat E 6th and carried forward unchanged.

21.4 One collateral test, re-pointed deliberately

ks1195 exists to test the no-Redis degrade path: it asserts isRedisAvailable() === false as a precondition, then used to pin that a connector create still answered 201 there. Both promises cannot hold — fail-closed and “201 while Redis is down” are contradictory. Two assertions were re-pointed to [503, 503, 429, 429, 429] and toBe(0), and that cell's title now states the new contract. These are the only assertion changes in this work. The DEGRADED / redis-not-ready assertions are untouched.

21.5 What this costs, and whose decision it was

The cost is stated rather than discovered: while Platform K’s Redis is down, Platform S cannot create documents through a connector — they answer 503. That was put to Kam as secuura-ks1256-redis-outage-stops-connector-creates-1006 and ruled a, “Accept: fail closed (503) during a Redis outage”: “Security first: no restricted document type slips through while the allow-list cannot be read. Cost: Platform-S cannot create documents while K’s Redis is down.”

21.6 Residue, named and NOT fixed here

The other readers of the same settings key were not audited: admin.ts:1119, :1144, :1154, health.ts:52 and verification.ts:1283. Each may carry the same fail-open shape. They are named here so the gap is on the record, not widened into this ticket. The fresh-install gap in 21.1 row 3 stays open by Kam’s ruling b.

24. A missing GENERATED Prisma client is diagnosed, not reported as a module error (KS-1305)

What this fixes. A fresh worktree installs @prisma/client but never generates it: npm ci runs with --ignore-scripts, so prisma generate does not run.
The bare require('@prisma/client') inside getPrismaClient() then throws Cannot find module '.prisma/client/default' — a module-resolution error that reads like a product defect in the originate service, and which cost real time to diagnose more than once.
The load now names the cause and the command that fixes it, and every other load error is rethrown untouched.

24.1 The mechanism, and what is deliberately NOT changed

The change is a pure insertion of 19 lines (numstat 19 0) immediately before the existing require. It loads @prisma/client once inside a try; on success the original require reads the module cache, so the happy path is byte-for-byte the same behaviour. db.ts is the tenant-isolation module — it holds withTenant, the GUC wrapper, getGucPrisma and createPoolProxy — and no GUC, tenant or RLS line is touched. The six KS 458 tenant-GUC cells are green at the head. The new message carries no environment or credential data; cause carries the resolver's error, which holds module paths only.

24.2 The guard is a three-term conjunction, and each term has its own red arm

The rewrite fires only when err?.code === 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND' and the message contains .prisma/client; anything else is throw err — the same object, not a copy. A guard with three terms needs three arms, or some term is being asserted by prose rather than by a cell.
ArmTerm it falsifiesResult
A — drop the message testmessage names .prisma/client C1 red (1 failed | 9 passed)
B — rethrow a NEW Errorthe same-object rethrow C1 and C3 red (2 failed | 8 passed)
C — drop the code testcode === 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND' C3 red (1 failed | 9 passed)
Arm C is why this block exists in this shape. Before C3 was added, Arm C left the suite at 10 passed — the code term was pinned by nothing.
D1 supplies a matching code and a matching message; C1 supplies a matching code and a non-matching message ('@prisma/client', an at-sign, not a dot).
No cell presented an error whose message matched while its code did not, so deleting the code test changed no verdict. C3 supplies exactly that error and requires the same object back.
Each arm was run with tsc rc 0 first: an arm that does not compile reports Tests: 0 total, which is a load failure, not an inert tamper, and proves nothing about the guard.

With the test file present and the product hunk reverted, the base gives 1 failed | 9 passed (10) — both numbers non-zero, so the red is a real red. The failure quotes the defect verbatim: expected substring the generated Prisma client (node_modules/.prisma/client) is missing, received Cannot find module '.prisma/client/default' from 'node_modules/@prisma/client/default.js'. At the head, 10 passed (10).

27. The tenant-isolation job's stderr goes to its own file, so a legitimate run's artefact stays parseable (KS-1436)

What this fixes. Blockchain/Testing/jobs/06-tenant-isolation.sh:71 ran its runner as > "$OUT" 2>&1, folding stderr into the same file as the JSON result.
The runner writes its result to stdout (tests/tenant-isolation/runner.ts:262) and its diagnostics to stderr (runner.ts:74, console.error("login failed for …")), so any stderr line corrupted the artefact.
This is reached on a routine run, not an error path: runner.ts:150-151 is a deliberate two-principal fallback (verifier@ || holder@), and whenever the first login cannot succeed the console.error line is emitted and the fallback proceeds as designed.
The job still exited 0, while :74 and :75 read the artefact through jq … 2>/dev/null || echo "?" — so the parse failure was swallowed and the job printed tested=? cross-tenant_findings=?.

27.1 Why it had to land before the aggregator change

Before KS 1136's change an unreadable artefact was reported as a clean scan, so a genuine cross-tenant finding on a fallback run read as no findings. After KS 1136 lands the aggregator reports the artefact as unreadable instead, which turns every routine verifier@-fallback run red with a false cause. That is why this one-line fix is the merge condition for that pull request and lands first. KS 1382 is a different line in the same file (:31, TARGET_BASE defaulting to slot 1's gateway) and is not addressed here.

27.2 The change, and what is deliberately NOT changed

One product line: 2>&1 becomes 2> "$OUT.stderr". The stderr content is kept, not discarded — it is the diagnostic that explains a fallback, and a 2>/dev/null variant is driven as its own red arm below. The file's Writes: header line (:23) is unchanged: the new sidecar is a diagnostic, not a declared artefact. The jq … || echo "?" swallow at :74-:75 is left in place; this ticket fixes the cause, not that symptom.

28. A present but unparseable security artefact is reported, not read as a clean scan (KS-1136)

What this fixes. 09-aggregate-report.sh reads each job's artefact with jq -r … 2>/dev/null (08 with a bare jq), so an artefact that exists but does not parse — a job that aborted mid-write — yielded zero findings and rc 0.
That is indistinguishable from a clean scan.
KS 878 had already guarded 04's artefact; every other job's block was silent.
Each present, unparseable artefact now gets its own HIGH finding, exactly as 04's does.

28.1 The mechanism, and what is deliberately NOT changed

The change is a pure insertion of 14 lines (numstat 14 0) after is_baselined() and before ALL_FINDINGS reads $TMP, so the new findings are in the aggregate rather than appended after it. It loops the seven unguarded jobs (01 02 03 05 06 07 08) and calls the file's existing emit. 04 is untouched: its KS 878 guard already fires and a second finding would double-count. No threshold, baseline, exit-code path or report writer is touched, and the finding text carries a filename only — no artefact contents, no environment. jq -e . is the test, so a valid JSON null or false also reads as unreadable; that side effect is named here because -e sets its exit status from the output value, not only from parseability.

28.2 The guard is a two-term conjunction, and each term has its own red arm

It fires only when the artefact [ -f ] and ! jq -e . succeeds on it. Two terms need two arms, or one of them is being asserted by prose rather than by a cell. Each arm was run with bash -n rc 0 first: an arm that does not parse prints no summary line at all, which is a load failure, not an inert tamper.
ArmTerm it falsifiesResult
A — drop [ -f "$_f" ] &&the artefact EXISTS 4 cells red (2 passed, 4 failed): a missing artefact is reported unreadable, which breaks both main cells and both well-formed controls
B — drop ! jq -e .it does NOT parse 2 cells red (4 passed, 2 failed): every present artefact is reported unreadable, so the two well-formed controls red

29. The formatting gate reads its “in this push” label literally, not as a regex (KS-998)

What this fixes. check-package-format.sh decided whether a red file belonged to the current push with printf '%s\n' "$changed_paths" | grep -qx "$full".
-x anchors the match but still treats $full as a basic regular expression, so a path containing . or a bracket expression matches a different file.
A red src/a.b.ts absent from the push matched src/aXb.ts that was present, and the gate billed the red to the wrong author; a real src/[id].ts in the push matched nothing and was labelled inherited.
The predicate is now grep -qxF: the path is compared as a literal string, which is what a path is.

29.1 The mechanism, and what is deliberately NOT changed

The product change is one line — grep -qx to grep -qxF at systemTest/scripts/check-package-format.sh:180, inside the hunk the payload opens at :177. It changes only which label a red file is printed with. The gate's verdict is untouched: a red package still fails, the exit code is unchanged, and the trailer still counts the same number of failures — three of the suite's eight cells are CONTROLs asserting exactly that. No threshold, no baseline, no manifest, no package list and no exit-code path is touched.

29.2 Red-first, and the figures

25. A child vitest’s verdict comes from its spawn outcome and its JSON report, never from its text (KS-1313)

What this fixes. childSuiteCounts read the child run’s totals by matching /Tests\s+(?:(\d+) failed \| )?(\d+) passed \((\d+)\)/ against the child’s human-readable stdout and stderr.
That pattern requires the word “passed”, so a real fail-only, skip-only or todo-only run matched nothing and the helper threw — the KS 1226 residue this ticket records.
Worse, a child killed by its own 180 s spawnSync timeout writes no summary at all, so whether it was read as a pass depended on what else happened to be in its output (KS 1326).
The helper now runs the child with --reporter=json --outputFile.json=<tmp> and reads numPassedTests / numFailedTests from the report.
Before the report is read at all, endedNormally refuses any child that did not end on its own — a spawn error, a signal, or an exit status other than 0 or 1 — so a killed child cannot read as a pass even beside a passing report.

25.1 Red-first, and the proof it is not a load failure

Measured at base 147ae442074c. Hunk 3 alone — the seven new cells without the new reader — gives rc 1, 7 failed | 3 passed (10), and all seven reds are R1–R7.
The cells red by assertion, not by a load error: each calls a reader() helper whose first act is expect(typeof countsFromSpawn).toBe('function'), and typeof on an undeclared identifier is the one JavaScript form that does not throw. Proved rather than assumed by reading the JSON report’s own totals: passed + failed = 10, so cells ran. 0 passed and 0 failed would have been a load failure and is explicitly not what happened. With the full patch: 10 passed, 0 failed, rc 0.

25.2 Two tamper arms, each red on its own cells

Each arm has a unique anchor (grep -c == 1) and the whole file was restored sha256-identical afterwards. Arm T1 — endedNormally forced to return true: 8 passed / 2 failed, and the two reds are exactly R1 (timeout-killed, status 143 + ETIMEDOUT) and R2 (ended by SIGTERM). Arm T2 — the text read restored inside childSuiteCounts: 9 passed / 1 failed, and the one red is R7, the cell that reads this file’s own source and asserts no result.stdout or result.stderr. Both arms reported passed + failed = 10, so neither was a load failure.

25.3 The fixtures were captured on vitest 4.1.9; the runner here is 5.0.3

Checked rather than assumed, because a parser is only as good as the output it was captured from. R6’s fixtures are labelled “captured from real vitest 4.1.9 JSON reports”. The runner resolved here is 5.0.3 — read from node_modules/vitest/package.json, matching the lockfile pin, and confirmed by the binary itself printing vitest/5.0.3 darwin-arm64 node-v24.7.0. A manifest range (^5.0.3) is not a resolution.
A real 5.0.3 report was captured from a child run with the payload’s own flags and every field the fixtures use was compared: numTotalTests, numPassedTests, numFailedTests, numPendingTests and numTodoTests are all present and numeric, and the two the product code destructures yield { passed: 3, failed: 7 }, which agrees with that run’s own 7 failed | 3 passed (10). A control field that does not exist reads absent, so the presence test discriminates. No field the code reads differs between the two versions.

25.4 Types, lint and the package suite

tsconfig.node.json is the config that checks tests/, and tsconfig.json does not cover this file at all. Established with tsc --listFilesOnly: the test file appears 1 time in tsconfig.node.json’s program and 0 times in tsconfig.json’s. tsc --noEmit -p tsconfig.node.json is rc 0, 0 bytes; a planted const x: number = "s" makes the same command rc 2, 168 bytes naming TS2322 at the planted line, so the green discriminates.
eslint rc 0 / 0 bytes, with a planted void undefined firing no-meaningless-void-operator at rc 1 / 392 bytes. prettier --check rc 0. The package unit suite moves 1353 passed / 1353 (248 suites) → 1360 passed / 1360 (249 suites), both runs rc 0 and 0 failed — the delta is this change’s seven cells in one new describe.

25.5 Not covered, and one hole named as a follow-up

A follow-up, not a regression: endedNormally accepts exit status 1, which vitest also uses for an unhandled error rather than ordinary test failures. So a child that died of an unhandled error while still writing a report with numFailedTests: 0 would be accepted. That is strictly narrower than the behaviour being replaced and is not made worse by this change, but it is a real remaining gap and is named here rather than discovered later.
This is a test-harness change: no service, no runtime, no migration, no deploy, and therefore no live sweep is owed. The earlier attempt #1245 is closed unmerged; it tried to repair the text parsing by label set, and its capturedChildOutput.ts helper is not needed once the verdict stops coming from text — its blob for this path differs from this one. 30. The transfer reject handler refuses a wrong-typed signature instead of running the reject (KS-1435)

30.1 What was wrong, and why a 200 was the worst possible answer

The published TransferRejectRequest declares signature as a string, but rejectTransferSchema in services/transfer/src/index.ts did not declare it at all. Zod strips keys a schema does not name, so a signature of the wrong type was not refused — it was silently discarded, the schema then validated, and the reject ran with 200. The caller gets a success for a request the published contract says is invalid, and the rejection is recorded without the signature it believed it had sent. A stripped field is worse than a rejected one precisely because nothing surfaces.

30.2 The fix is one declaration, and optional() is the load-bearing half

signature: z.string().optional(), added to rejectTransferSchema. Typed, so a non-string is now a validation error and the handler answers 400. optional() keeps the field not required, which is what the contract says and what every existing caller relies on: making it mandatory would have reddened the pre-existing reject cells that send no signature at all. The narrowing is the type, never the presence.

30.3 Red-first, and the red is an assertion rather than a load failure

With the test hunk applied alone and the product file untouched at the base, the suite gives rc 1, 2 failed | 77 passed (79). Both failures read AssertionError: expected 200 to be 400 — the defect reproduced by its own symptom, not a module that would not import. That distinction is the point of running the test hunk first: a compile-breaking tamper reds with 0 passed and 0 failed, which is a load failure and proves nothing about the guard. Here 77 cells still pass around the two that fail.
CellSendsBase (test only)Head (test + fix)
TR1 — an object signature is refused with 400 and the transfer stays pending signature: {}RED, expected 200 to be 400 green
TR2 — a numeric signature is refused with 400 signature: 42RED, expected 200 to be 400 green
TRC1 (control) — a string signature is accepted and the reject runs signature: '0xabc123'greengreen
TRC1 is green on both sides, proved by name rather than by arithmetic. vitest run -t 'TRC1' reads 1 passed | 78 skipped, rc 0, at the base and at the head. A control that is only green on one side cannot tell a real narrowing from a schema that started refusing everything, so TR1 and TR2 going red while TRC1 holds is what attributes the red to the wrong type and not to the field's presence.

30.5 An idempotence control that does NOT fire here, and why it is recorded rather than claimed

Re-applying the test section after it is already applied succeeds, rc 0, on the working tree and through apply --cached against a temp index at the base. git apply --check -v says Hunk #1 succeeded at 938 (offset -39 lines): the hunk's only context is two closing-brace lines, which recur throughout a test file, so git apply cannot tell the patch from a fresh insertion elsewhere. 35. Job 04 fails a scan when trivy reports neither Results nor ArtifactName (KS-1274)

35.1 What this row is, and what it is not

KS 1136 already made job 04 treat a non-zero trivy exit, or output jq could not read, as a FAILED scan. What it did not catch is a trivy that exits 0 and prints a well-formed but empty object. A bare {} parses cleanly, carries no findings, and so was recorded as a clean image — the one shape where "no vulnerabilities" and "no scan happened" are indistinguishable from the artefact. This row adds the missing guard at Blockchain/Testing/jobs/04-container-trivy.sh:115-120: the scan is recorded scan-failed when stdout has neither Results nor ArtifactName.

35.2 The ticket's own suggested fix is wrong as written

The ticket proposes failing on a missing Results key. That over-fires. A genuinely clean image can report ArtifactName with no Results array at all, and failing it would turn every clean scan into an error. The guard therefore requires both keys to be absent, and the suite pins that distinction with a control cell — CONTROL KS-1274 a clean report with ArtifactName and no Results stays clean: rc 0, no error — which passes in the patched state and in the reverted state, so it cannot be mistaken for the cell under test.

35.3 Why the three suites' clean stub had to move with the guard

All three trivy suites stubbed a clean image as {}. Under the new guard {} is precisely the failure case, so left alone every clean-path cell in all three suites would have started failing for the right reason in the wrong test. The stub becomes {"Results":[]} in the same commit — a real clean report rather than an empty one. The fail.txt vocabulary gains bare and nores so the stub can produce each shape deliberately.

35.4 Red-first, and what is still owed

Red proof by reverting the product only, suites kept patched. 04-container-trivy.sh restored to the base blob and container_trivy_failed_scan_is_loud.test.sh re-run: 4 passed, 1 failed, rc 1, the single failure being 🔴 KS-1274 a trivy that exits 0 with a bare {} is recorded as scan-failed and the job exits 1, with the control cell green in both states. Product restored byte-identical (sha256/16 b0a19e77c940633c). Green after: 5/0, 6/0, 5/0 across the three suites. A live run is owed — this host has no docker daemon and no trivy binary, so every cell runs against stubs on a private PATH and the real scanner's bare-{} behaviour is UNMEASURED here. The ticket does not move to Done.

36. The api-gateway stopped answering 500s that carry the thrown error's own text (KS-1410)

36.1 What this row is, and what it is not

Ten catch blocks across three api-gateway routers answered res.status(500).json({ ... message: err.message || 'Internal server error' }) with no NODE_ENV guard, so whatever the thrown error said — a driver message, a constraint name, a path — reached the client in every environment, production included. Each router now has a local fail500 helper, the shape originate already uses (KS 1334, KS 730): log the thrown text server-side with the route named, answer a constant INTERNAL_ERROR body. Sites: six in routes/notifications.ts, three in routes/batch.ts, one in routes/audit-export.ts. This is 10 of the ticket's 28 sites; the other 18 stay OPEN, including transfer/delegations.ts.

37. The smoke test survives its own first check under errexit (KS-1139)

37.1 The defect, and why it hid on this machine

pass(), fail() and warn() in Blockchain/Dev/scripts/smoke-test.sh counted with ((PASS++)). A post-increment from 0 evaluates to 0, so the arithmetic command returns status 1. The script runs under set -euo pipefail, and bash 4.1 and later apply errexit to (( )) — so on a Linux runner or the Ubuntu demo VM the script died at its FIRST check and printed nothing after it. macOS /bin/bash 3.2.57, which is what this host ships, ignores that status, which is exactly why it passed locally and was unusable as a deploy check. All three helpers now use X=$((X + 1)), which never returns non-zero.

37.2 Red-first, and what the surviving cells mean

The new suite reads each helper's counter statement out of smoke-test.sh and drives the script under errexit. At the base: 3 passed, 3 failed, rc 1. With the fix: 6 passed, 0 failed, rc 0. The three that pass in BOTH states are the controls — a degraded run still counts, a down service still fails — and the total staying at 6 across both arms is what shows the cells executed rather than the suite failing to load. The sibling smoke_test_degraded_warns.test.sh reads 5 passed, 0 failed, unchanged.

37.3 What this row does NOT prove

The defect only bites on bash >= 4.1. This host has no such shell — /bin/bash is 3.2.57 — so the failing-before behaviour was never reproduced here; it is read from the shell's documented errexit semantics and corroborated by a reviewer's own rc-1 measurement on bash 5.2, which is his figure, not mine. A run on bash >= 4.1 is owed, and the ticket does not move to Done. The three scripts/validate-env.sh sites named in review are out of scope here and still OPEN: they need their own ticket and their own pass.

38. Six nft request bodies are marked required in the published contract, and the contract is REGENERATED, never hand-patched (KS-1449)

38.1 What this row is, and what it is not

Six operations declared a requestBody without required: true, so a spec-driven caller (Schemathesis) sent no body at all and counted the request valid; each handler's zod safeParse then answered 400 and the run failed positive_data_acceptance. This row marks all six required in services/nft-certificate/src/nft-certificate.openapi.ts: POST /api/nft/mint, POST /api/nft/ipfs/upload, PUT /api/nft/admin/platform-fee, POST /api/nft/ipfs/pin, POST /api/nft/ipfs/unpin and POST /api/nft/metadata/estimate-size. It is the spec half only: the runtime half — each handler's own 400 on an absent body — is READ from the source, never driven, because this host has no running stack. The ticket does not move to Done.

38.2 Red-first, with real assertion reds

Two new suites render the document the generator publishes, from the shared registry the nft-certificate module populates on import — no server, no database, no network. At the base the service suite reads 48 passed (48). With the two test files and no product change it reads 6 failed | 54 passed (60), the six reds being NM1-NM3 and NP1-NP3 as AssertionErrors on requestBody.required. With the product hunks applied it reads 60 passed (60), tsc rc 0. Red before, green after, on this worktree, with the numbers quoted.

38.3 The published contract is GENERATED — and the Spark YAML companions MISLAND

Blockchain/Dev/docs/openapi/secuura-api.yaml is written by Blockchain/Dev/scripts/generate-openapi.ts. Each Spark pass also ships an openapi-yaml.companion.diff, and those diffs are a trap. They are cut against spec blob 52310cab1; develop carries 146bae7edb87, +87 lines on. Their hunk context is generic (security / requestBody: / content: / application/json:), so git apply places them by offset search on the nearest matching operation. Measured at this base: all twelve apply rc 0 and five land required: true on the WRONG operation — among them this row's own nft-ipfs-pin-unpin-size, which alone flips POST /api/nft/ipfs/upload instead of POST /api/nft/ipfs/unpin.
So the YAML here is produced by npm run generate-openapi and proved structurally: parse base and head, compare every paths[p][m].requestBody.required. Result: exactly the six declared operations flipped, 0 flipped off, 0 operations added or removed, 145 request-bodied operations before and after, and the whole 40,021-line document differs by 6 added lines, 0 removed, every one a required: line. npm run check:openapi is rc 1 with the product change and the old YAML, and rc 0 after regenerating.

38.4 A control that does NOT discriminate here, named so nobody reuses it

The intended firing control is: build the YAML from the real companions and watch the structural reader refuse it. For this row it does not fire. Applied as a pair, the two companions' displaced hunks cancel: the result is byte-identical to the generated file (cmp rc 0) and check:openapi reads rc 0, because the operation one companion mislands onto — ipfs/upload — is itself in this row's op set. The control fires only on the mislanding companion applied alone against its own three intended operations: the reader then exits 2 naming unexpected ['post /api/nft/ipfs/upload'] and missing ['post /api/nft/ipfs/unpin'], and check:openapi reads rc 1. The lesson is that the companion route was right here by luck, and nothing in that route tells a reader which case they are in.
