42. stack_guard lists a project ONCE when its containers disagree about the owner (KS-1355)

42.1 What this row is, and what it is not

stack_guard.sh groups foreign stacks by (project, owner). A project whose containers carry different owner labels therefore produced one line per distinct owner, so a single foreign stack could be reported twice and the operator could not tell one project from two. This row makes a project print ONE line. Where some containers carry a real owner and others carry owner=unknown, the line names the real owner and appends the unknown count. NARROWING: this is KS-1355 spot 1 only and the ticket does NOT close — the stack tooling's other non-slot-derived spots are untouched.

A reader upgrading past this commit sees different output for one input. A project with two DIFFERENT real owners now prints one line — the first (project, owner) tuple in docker ps order — where the tip printed both. That is a deliberate consequence of "one line per project", not an oversight: the second real owner is no longer shown. The (+N container(s) with owner unknown) wording is this change's own choice; the ticket asks only that an unknown count be appended.

44. transfer-custody resolves a holder email inside originate, not through auth's lookup (KS-1402)

44.1 What this row is, and what it is not

POST /api/documents/:id/transfer-custody with newHolderEmail no longer calls auth's GET /api/users/lookup. That call forwarded the caller's credential, and Platform S's connector key is minted without users:read on purpose, so every S custody transfer by email answered 403 (Stuart measured 7 of 7 on 2026-10-05). Originate now computes the email's lookup HMAC and reads users itself, on the request's db, with the tenant bound in the query. Kam's ruling (card secuura-ks1402-s-key-cannot-carry-users-read-1006, choice a): "Originate resolves the holder with its own service credential (Stuart's option 2)." Reading "its own service credential" as originate's own database role, rather than a new service token, is a reading of that sentence, confirmed by Wednesday on 2026-10-09. No token is minted, stored or sent, auth is not changed, and no scope moves. The act is still authorised on the caller, first, by the unchanged documents:transfer-custody gate; only resolution moved. Section 9a (KS-1402's first half, auth's /lookup accepting a connector token) still describes auth correctly; this route simply no longer goes there.

44.2 The headline for the gate: the tenant guard is newly load-bearing for connectors

Before KS-1402 auth refused the connector before its tenant compare ever ran, so for a connector the cross-tenant guard was unreachable. Now the connector resolves, and the bound tenant predicate is the only thing between it and another tenant's user. Cell C2 pins it: a tenant-A connector naming an email whose only user is in tenant B gets 404 RECIPIENT_NOT_FOUND, byte-equal to a true miss, nothing written, and the tenant value bound is tenant A (asserted as a value, not as SQL text). C2b pins the same guard for an interactive caller, which did reach auth's compare at base: green at base and head. The bound predicate is also stricter than the path it replaces: auth's /lookup skipped its tenant compare whenever the caller's credential carried no tenant (the KS 1406 class, filed, unchanged here).

48.2 The one answer that is kept on purpose

An id that passes the format pattern but is not a UUID (e.g. 0) answered 200 [] before, because the swallow hid the ::uuid cast error. It still answers 200 [], and the query is now not run for it, so the cast cannot turn into a 500. The check is the file's own UUID_PATTERN (canonical hyphenated form, case-insensitive), the same pattern the four sibling routes use through rejectInvalidWebhookId. Moving such ids to 404, as those routes do, is a contract decision for another ticket. Read, not tested: a 32-hex id written without hyphens, which Postgres would cast, now also gets 200 [] instead of its rows.

45. api-gateway fail500 logs a thrown object's type and field names, not [object Object] (KS-1346)

45.1 What this row is, and what it is not

Three api-gateway routers share one fail500() helper: routes/notifications.ts, routes/batch.ts and routes/audit-export.ts. Its log expression was String(err), so a thrown non-Error object rendered as "[object Object]" and the throw's content was lost from the log. It now logs a thrown object's type and field names only. Kam's ruling (card secuura-ks1346-logging-thrown-objects-leaks-secrets, choice a): "log a thrown object's TYPE and FIELD NAMES only." The expression is byte-for-byte the one already live in services/originate/src/routes/adminConfig.ts (263 bytes, cmp rc 0 against all three sites after the change; a cmp against the pre-ruling text differs, as the control). The 500 response body is unchanged — it was already the constant INTERNAL_ERROR body, so the response tells a reader nothing about this row.

45.2 What it deliberately does NOT change, because the expression's own branches decide it

A thrown Error still logs its .message. Thrown text is still logged verbatim (typeof err === 'string' ? err). An empty Error("") logs "". Only objects, class instances and numbers are reduced to type plus field names. QA gate77 threw a credential-shaped URL at these routes and it reached logger.error intact. That case is recorded on this ticket and is not closed by this row, so nothing here should be read as "the log no longer carries secrets". The three sites were added on 2026-10-09 with blobs 5ae6c0788dfd, 75e84b3aa06c and 893669657db0; the same three paths at this row's base 613070f29112 carry those identical blobs, so the change lands on exactly the sites QA measured.

Whole api-gateway suite 95 files, 860 passed, 0 failed; tsc --noEmit rc 0 with no output; eslint src rc 0 with 0 errors (36 pre-existing warnings, none in a file this row touches). The four platform suites were NOT run — they need a booted local stack this seat does not have, so no figure from them is quoted. A live run is owed: this changes runtime logging behaviour, and the ticket does not move to Done on offline green. Measured by Seat R 28th, 2026-10-10, on node v24.7.0 / vitest 4.1.11.

46. audit-export 502 answers a constant message, and logs the failed fetch by the ruled expression (KS-1410)

46.1 What this row is, and what it is not

GET /api/admin/audit/export in api-gateway (routes/audit-export.ts): when the fetch to the security service throws, the 502 body was `Failed to reach security service: ${err.message}` with no NODE_ENV guard, so the thrown text reached the client in every environment. It now answers the constant Failed to reach security service, and the catch logs the failure server-side, naming the route. Before, that catch logged nothing. This is one site of KS-1410's scope (the ticket counts 28 across six services), and the ticket stays open. Raised from a Wednesday-held Spark pass and re-proved on develop 613070f29112. The file's own fail500 at :24-25 is not changed here: PR 1443 (KS 1346) carries that line, about 145 lines away from this hunk.

46.2 The log line uses the ruled expression, and what it still logs

The new log line's error value is the expression Kam ruled on 2026-09-27 (card secuura-ks1346-logging-thrown-objects-leaks-secrets, choice a: log a thrown object's type and field names only). It is byte-identical to the ruled line in originate/src/routes/adminConfig.ts:104: 262 bytes, sha256/16 4623660d465c942a, compared with cmp. What it reduces and what it does not: an Error is logged as its .message and a thrown string as it is; a plain object or class instance is logged as thrown <Type> with fields [a, b]; any other value as thrown <typeof>. So at this site the 502 body no longer carries the thrown text, while the log still carries an Error's message. The Spark's payload logged err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err), which writes a plain object as [object Object] (node v24.7.0); replacing it is the one deviation from that payload.

47. transfer's process-expired 500 logs the thrown text server-side instead of returning it (KS-1410)

50. The re-link guard accepts relative re-link destinations and uid-0 users with a group (KS-937)

What this fixes. Two false BLOCKs in Blockchain/Dev/scripts/check-shared-relink.sh, assertion A (the re-link invariant). This carries KS-937 items F-C and F-E; F-A, F-B, F-D and F-F are untouched and the ticket does not move to Done.
F-C: the re-link destination had to be node_modules/… or an absolute /…/node_modules/…, so ./node_modules/@secuura/shared and app/node_modules/@secuura/shared read as “final stage has NO re-link”. The prefix group no longer requires a leading slash.
F-E: USER root:root and USER 0:0 were compared whole, so they read as non-root and the re-link after them was refused on the privilege rule. The :group part is now dropped before the comparison, when a user part is present.

50.1 One deviation from the Spark payload

Ruled, one line. The payload dropped :group unconditionally. For USER :root (an empty user part) that left an empty value, which the guard treats as root. Nothing has measured that USER :root runs as root, or that Docker builds it, so the group is dropped only when a user part is present (if (u !~ /^:/)) and one cell pins USER :root to the privilege refusal.

50.3 What the guard still refuses (the widening, measured)

32 probe Dockerfiles, base guard against this guard. 5 accepted by both, 9 newly accepted (./, app/, x/y/z/, $APP/ and ../ prefixes; USER root:root, 0:0, root:1000, 0:secuura), 18 refused by both, 0 newly refused.
Refused by both: a wrong package name, a wrong source, a hard link, a link before the last node_modules write, a link after USER secuura, no link, and USER secuura:root, 1000:0, node:node, rootless:root, root0:root, :root, :0, ${UID}:${GID}. The 66 refusal cells declared in the base suite (static count: expect 28, row_case 31, nonjs_case 7) all pass at the head, 66 of 66.
A measured gap, not fixed here: ../node_modules/@secuura/shared (the parent of WORKDIR) is newly accepted. 54. ApiKeyCreateRequest declares the rotate flag that POST /api/security/keys acts on (KS-1434)

What this fixes. The create handler for POST /api/security/keys accepts rotate (z.boolean().optional().default(false) in the create schema in services/security/src/index.ts, added under KS 577). With a connectorId it retires that connector’s other active keys once the new key is minted.
The published request schema, ApiKeyCreateRequest, listed eight properties and not rotate, so an integrator reading the contract, and a spec-driven caller such as Schemathesis, could not see the field or send it.

53. The preflight clean-room leg prints which tracked lockfiles it did not install (KS-1426)

What this adds. Blockchain/Dev/scripts/preflight/lockfile-cleanroom.sh (preflight leg 2) prints All N standalone lock(s) pass clean-room npm ci.. The N counts the locks that a find over four directories (services packages frontend scripts) reaches. A new function, report_surface, runs after that line when the leg was started with no arguments. It asks git for the tracked package-lock.json files, prints how many of them the leg installed, and lists the paths of the rest. 61. Leg 14’s comment filter is pinned by a fixture hook carrying a commented control (KS-1746)

What this pins. Blockchain/Dev/scripts/preflight/preflight.sh:722 is the filter — grep -vE '^[[:space:]]*#' "$hook_src" — feeding :723, which extracts ${NAME:- reads from the pre-push hook so leg 14 can strip them before running the shell suites. A control named only inside a comment must not be derived and must not be stripped. Nothing asserted that, and the tier-1 gate’s mutant G2 (delete the filter stage) survived preflight_deps.test.sh at 68/0.
No product file changes. The ticket is a missing cell, not a wrong filter: the code’s own comment at :709-713 states the hardening has no behaviour change on today’s hook, and that statement was re-measured here and is accurate. preflight.sh hashes bae62e73e2b087142b0c1fec1a9fedb155259d53907db5459e806e3d756a99f5 before and after this change.
The whole change is one file, Blockchain/Dev/scripts/__tests__/preflight_deps.test.sh: a third hook-stub mode on the existing preflight_fixture_run fixture, one extra reporting line in the fixture stub suite, and seven cells. .dockerignore:14 is **/__tests__, so the file reaches no image; of 35 Dockerfiles the only COPY lines naming scripts are originate’s run-migrations.sh (:47, :67) and auth’s own services/auth/scripts (:67), with 286 COPY lines across those Dockerfiles as the positive control that the matcher works.

61.1 Why no cell was possible against the real hook

The behaviour is unobservable on the shipped hook. On .githooks/pre-push the only ${NAME:- match is live code at :77 (if [ "${ALLOW_FORCE:-0}" = "1" ]; then), so excluding comment lines yields the identical derived set [ALLOW_FORCE]. With the filter present or absent the output is the same, which is exactly why G2 survived every one of the 68 cells. A cell therefore cannot be written against the real hook at all; it needs a hook that carries a commented control, and no fixture mode wrote one.
The new commented mode writes a hook with both: a comment line beginning with # that names a control the hook never reads, and the live ALLOW_FORCE read. The derived set must stay [ALLOW_FORCE]; with the filter gone it becomes [ALLOW_FORCE FAKE], because the derivation ends in sort -u and FAKE sorts second. The commented line must start with #: that is what the filter keys on, and a ${NAME:- inside a trailing comment is not excluded.

61.2 Two oracles, and why the behavioural one needs FAKE set

The announcement alone would not have been enough. Oracle (a) is the line leg 14 prints: the derived set must read exactly ALLOW_FORCE, asserted as a whole line so an extra name, a missing name or a reworded line all fail. But this is leg 14 describing its own work, and that is precisely what the earlier mutant M3 (announce the controls, strip nothing) was able to fake while surviving the gate at 61/61.
Oracle (b) is read from the stripped side, in the shape KS 1643’s Minor 2 established for ALLOW_FORCE: FAKE=1 is placed in the caller’s environment and the fixture stub suite must still see it, because a commented control is never added to env_clear. The stub reports its own environment, so this does not read leg 14’s words.
Why (b) needs FAKE SET. env -u on a variable that is already unset is indistinguishable from not stripping it, so an unset probe reads <unset> on the real tree and under G2 and discriminates nothing. One cell asserts that vacuity directly — with FAKE unset the probe reads <unset> either way — so a later edit cannot quietly simplify the FAKE=1 out of the arm above it and leave a dead test behind.

62. The suite whose comments are graded by a sibling now says so (KS-1750)

The obvious draft breaks the thing it documents. The committed notice therefore describes each string by its role and its required count, and says in-line why it does not quote them.

63. generated_guard_restore keeps the suite's own exit status when a cleanup is chained in front of it (KS-1738)

What this fixes. systemTest/__tests__/support/generated_guard.sh’s generated_guard_restore() captures the suite’s exit status as its FIRST statement (local rc=$?) so a failed restore can re-raise it. That works when the guard IS the EXIT trap. It does not work when a suite chains its own cleanup in front of it: the chained command runs first and overwrites $?.
systemTest/__tests__/bootstrap_login_diagnosis.test.sh did exactly that — trap 'stop_stub; generated_guard_restore' EXIT. stop_stub succeeds, so $? was 0 by the time the guard read it, the guard took its “the suite itself passed” branch, and a suite that exited 3 was reported as 1. LOW severity, and stated as such: a failed restore is still reported and still exits non-zero, and the runner still scores the suite as failed — only the distinction between “the suite failed” and “the restore failed” is lost.
The ticket listed three shapes and chose none. Shape 3 (“leave it”) was ruled out by Wednesday; shapes 1 and 2 together were chosen by the builder and ratified. Shape 1 is the fix (an optional status argument), shape 2 is the constraint written down at the guard’s header and at the chained call site — because the ticket’s own risk statement is that chaining is the natural thing for the next suite to do.

63.1 The shape, and why the ticket's own suggested call-site form was NOT used

Opt-in, so no existing caller changes behaviour. generated_guard_restore now PREFERS a status passed as its first argument over $?. local rc=$? stays the first statement — any command before it, [ included, overwrites $? — and the argument is applied immediately after. With no argument the behaviour is byte-for-byte the old one, which is why the two inline copies and every plain-trap caller are untouched.
The chained call site becomes trap 'rc=$?; stop_stub; generated_guard_restore "$rc"' EXIT: the cleanup still runs FIRST, and the real status is handed in. The ticket’s literal shape-1 suggestion was trap 'generated_guard_restore $?; stop_stub' EXIT, and that was deliberately not used: on a failed restore the guard exits, so putting the guard first would mean stop_stub never runs on exactly the path the guard exists for — it would leak the login-stub listener that KS 1201 was filed about. That reasoning was put to Wednesday and ratified as reasoning; the gate judges whether the code does it.
A non-numeric argument is REFUSED by name and falls back to $?, rather than being used: exit "$rc" on a non-number is a shell error, which would trade a wrong status for no status at all. That branch has its own cell.

63.2 Red-first as three arms, and the ticket's table reproduced independently

Measured at base c3eb63c9d23b, 2026-10-27, Kamil’s MacBook Pro. Node v26.8.1, npm 11.19.0, GNU bash 3.2.57(1)-release (arm64-apple-darwin26). The guard is a sourced file that installs an EXIT trap, so every arm drives it in a CHILD bash process with its OWN $FIXTURES directory; no cell reads or writes the repo’s real systemTest/fixtures/generated. The instrument is the suite’s existing fake cp, first on PATH, which fails only for a destination ending /generated/.
Three arms, each a distinct (suite, guard) pair, fingerprinted so the arms cannot be confused: BEFORE = original suite + original guard → 15 passed, 0 failed, rc 0. RED = new suite + original guard → 18 passed, 2 failed, rc 1. AFTER = new suite + new guard → 20 passed, 0 failed, rc 0. The two cells red in the RED arm are exactly the two that depend on the fix: the chained-with-status arm (rc=1, want 3, because the old guard ignores its argument) and the non-numeric refusal (the old guard prints no such message).
The ticket’s A/B/C table is reproduced here rather than quoted. A, plain trap with a failing restore → 3, own status preserved. B, chained with NO status passed → 1, own status lost. C, chained with a SUCCEEDING restore → 3. A against B isolates the chaining; C isolates the failed-restore path, so chaining alone is not what breaks it. All three are green in BOTH the RED and AFTER arms, which is the point: they measure the chaining, not the fix. B stays at 1 after the fix on purpose — shape 1 is opt-in, so a call site that passes nothing still flattens the status, and that is precisely why shape 2 writes the constraint down.
An independent check the ticket invited: it records the guard text it measured as sha256 6ee51a49…. The original guard in this tree hashes 6ee51a497cc0863ff1ad21c5936c72b4cb1c7216e62a6e58cb7c5430941f2d2f — so the ticket’s fingerprint matches the file this change starts from, and its table was measured against the same object. 65. The “run compared as one value” guard sees objects, reversed arrays and split arrays, and the REAL cell’s summary is a predicate that can fail (KS-1529)

What this fixes. Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/__tests__/ks1000-auth-test-files-are-type-checked-against-a-shrinking-baseline.test.ts pins the behaviour of the type-check ratchet (scripts/typecheck-tests/check.cjs). The Sonnet-tier gate on PR 1514 (KS 1519) returned GO WITH NOTE — 0 Major, 3 Minor — and two of the Minors needed a change in this file. (a) The guard that keeps a cell from comparing a checker run as ONE value was the regex /expect\(\[[^\]]*\.status[^\]]*\.out/ tested line by line, so three shapes the gate planted all passed with 35 of 35 green: an object, a reversed array and an array split over several lines.
(b) The gate’s mutant M3 reduced the REAL cell (REAL: services/auth against the committed baseline passes…) to a bare status check, dropping the summary string it expects: 35 of 35 stayed green. The exposure predates 1514 — the cell before it had the same one.
(a) is now runsComparedAsOneValue (module scope): it scans the JOINED text, opens on [ or {, takes the two fields in either order, and is bounded by the first ] or }. The ticket’s own first suggestion bounded the scan by ), and the ticket measured that blind spot itself: a nested call BEFORE the first field ends the scan. A cell plants exactly that shape. Every shape is planted in a COPY of this file’s own text, so the cell shows the guard reading THIS file. (b) is a named constant, AUTH_GREEN_SUMMARY, a cell that proves it can fail, and a cell that reads the REAL cell off the syntax tree to prove it still passes it.

65.1 The ticket’s own shape for (b) does not kill M3 on its own

Measured, not argued. The ticket’s fix shape — a named constant used by the REAL cell and a cell that feeds a red run through expectRun(red, 0, <the constant>) — was built first: AUTH_GREEN_SUMMARY, and one cell that hands it a red run, a SILENT run (right status, summary gone) and a wrong-status run. M3 was then applied to a COPY of the finished file with the pin cell below EXCLUDED: 83 passed, 0 red, rc 0 across the whole file. The constant proves the predicate CAN fail; it does not watch the REAL cell’s source, so a cell that stops using it is invisible.
What kills it. A cell reads the REAL cell off the syntax tree (the typescript compiler API, as the ks1480 and ks1564 guards do) and requires a call expectRun(<run>, 0, AUTH_GREEN_SUMMARY) naming the constant. The ticket names the weakness of a source-text check — it passes when the call is commented out — and the syntax tree has no comments in it. Five controls inside that cell mutate the REAL cell’s own text and each must read zero such calls: M3, the call commented out, the constant inlined back as a literal, another status, the call removed. With the pin in place, M3 reds the pin cell, and the other 83 cells of the file (the number measured above) stay green.

66. Leg 14’s hook-control refusal has a cell for each of its two arms, and the empty-set fixture now models the empty set (KS-1756)

What this pins. Blockchain/Dev/scripts/preflight/preflight.sh:731 refuses to run the shell suites when the derived set of the pre-push hook’s control variables is empty ([ -z "$hook_controls" ]) or is non-empty but does not contain ALLOW_FORCE. The fixture mode nocontrol in preflight_deps.test.sh was written to reproduce the first, and its comment said so, but its hook line began with : rather than #. The comment filter at :722 drops only lines that start with #, so the line was kept and NAME was derived. No cell in the shell-suite tree drove an empty derivation, and a condition that let one through passed this suite at 75/0.
No product file changes. preflight.sh hashes bae62e73e2b087142b0c1fec1a9fedb155259d53907db5459e806e3d756a99f5 before and after. The whole change is one file, Blockchain/Dev/scripts/__tests__/preflight_deps.test.sh: the nocontrol hook line now starts with #, the old line is kept verbatim as a new mode trailingcomment, and seven cells tell the two arms apart. .dockerignore:14 is **/__tests__, so the file reaches no image.
Both arms classify as HOOKCTL-REFUSED/1, so the verdict cannot tell them apart. The refusal’s own line can: Derived: [ ] - expected to contain ALLOW_FORCE. for the empty set and Derived: [NAME ] - expected to contain ALLOW_FORCE. for the non-empty one. Each is asserted as a whole line (grep -cxF), and each has a control that the other arm’s output must read 0 on, so the two cannot be reading the same line.

66.1 Why the old arm is kept, not replaced

Replacing nocontrol outright would have lost a kill. Before this change the non-empty arm was exercised by accident, through the misnamed fixture, and four existing cells depended on it. Making nocontrol truly empty and nothing else would have left a mutant that deletes the second half of the condition (M_2nd, leaving only -z) alive, because an empty set is refused either way. The old line is therefore kept verbatim as trailingcomment and given its own cells, which also pins a boundary of the filter that had no cell: a ${NAME:- in a trailing comment is not excluded.
The three existing call sites of nocontrol (HOOKCTL-REFUSED/1, the short-circuit, and the KS-1643 withheld-run cells) now run on the arm their comments describe — “the derivation has stopped working” — and stay green at 82/0.

66.2 The -z disjunct cannot be pinned, and why

It is redundant, so deleting it is an equivalent mutant. For an empty set the second half of the condition is also true: printf '%s\n' "" | grep -qx 'ALLOW_FORCE' fails, and the ! makes that a refusal. So [ -z "$hook_controls" ] || … and the same condition with the first half removed refuse on exactly the same inputs. A truth table over five derived sets ([], [NAME], [ALLOW_FORCE], [ALLOW_FORCE FAKE], [FAKE]) under bash 3.2 with pipefail, which is preflight.sh:91’s own setting, gives identical columns for the original and the deletion.
Driven through the real suite as a matched pair, the deletion arm reads 82 passed, 0 failed and a cell-by-cell verdict diff against the control moves zero cells. No cell can distinguish the disjunct’s presence, so a cell that “goes red when it is deleted” cannot exist. What a cell can do is make the branch execute, which the empty arm now does, and pin the two mutants that are not equivalent.
The two killable mutants separate cleanly by arm. M_accept (an empty set is accepted: [ -n "$hook_controls" ] && ! …) proceeds only on the empty set, and is killed by the empty arm. M_2nd (only -z remains) proceeds on [NAME] and [FAKE], and is killed by the trailing-comment arm. Whether to delete the redundant disjunct from preflight.sh is a product-file question and is not decided here.

68. The ks1186 test runs every control against every site, the stale “unawaited” comment is gone, and listUsers answers a DB fault like its siblings (KS-1484)

What this fixes. Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/repositories/userRepo.ts:372-373 said “The five sibling reads below still return fromRow unawaited: KS-1186”. That stopped being true when KS 1186 merged: the five sites read return await fromRow( at :449 :515 :588 :597 :630 at this base — getUserByIdWithPasswordHash, getUserByIdPreAuth, the two arms of getUserByEmail, getUserBySocialId. The sentence now says so and records what it used to say. Comment-only.
Three controls in services/auth/src/__tests__/ks1186-userrepo-fromrow-sites-are-awaited.test.ts were thin (the Opus gate on PR 1477): the non-infrastructure control ran against getUserByIdPreAuth alone; the no-fault control reached getUserByEmail only through its legacy arm, because the default mock answers the hash query with no rows; and the test did not assert that the repository logs the error, which the KS 999 test does for getUserById.
One table of the five sites now drives three families of cells. An infrastructure fault becomes ServiceUnavailable (5, as before, plus the log assertion). A non-infrastructure fault is rethrown as-is (5; checked by identity with toBe rather than by message, and logged). With nothing rejecting, each site resolves the row and logs no error (5; the hash arm is reached by priming the first query answer). 7 → 15 cells.
Item 3 — a BEHAVIOUR CHANGE on the user-listing path. listUsersInner ended in return Promise.all(result.rows.map((r) => fromRow(r))) with no catch, so a database fault while listing users answered the raw error, a subject-DEK read inside fromRow included. It now has the lookups’ contract: the SELECT and the per-row reads sit in one try; the catch logs DB listUsers failed; an infrastructure fault becomes a ServiceUnavailableError (503) and anything else is rethrown as-is. On GET /api/users and GET /api/users/admin/list that is a 503 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE where it was a 500 INTERNAL_ERROR — read, not run: both routes catch (error) { next(error); } and the error handler answers an AppError with its own status and a raw Error with 500.
The SELECT is inside the try, which is wider than the ticket’s example (the DEK read). That is how the lookups above are written, and a catch over only the per-row reads would leave one function classifying half of its faults. A cell fails if the SELECT is moved out; narrowing is a four-line move if a ruling prefers it.

69. The two N3 cells now assert that the hash they send is a real one (KS-1634)

What this fixes. In Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/__tests__/ks1634-v2-chain-only-match-carries-simulated.test.ts the two N3 cells (simulated as the string "true", and as the number 1) each send a real tx hash on purpose. Each cell now builds its reply first and asserts expect(reply.txHash).toMatch(REAL_TX_SHAPE) before sending it. REAL_TX_SHAPE is /^[0-9a-f]{64}$/, held apart from REAL_TX so a mock-prefixed value swapped into REAL_TX itself cannot satisfy it. The file goes 249 to 260 lines and keeps its 10 cells; two assertions are added, no cell is added or removed. No product file changes.

70. The KS-1347 proxy probe reads the subject’s imports as statements, not as one line shape (KS-1560)

What this pins. Blockchain/Dev/scripts/__tests__/ks1347_proxy_out_dir_spaced_checkout.test.sh plants the capture proxy’s OUT_DIR expression in a probe module and runs it. The probe inherits server.ts’s node: imports so that deleting one from server.ts reds the suite. The inherited set was read with grep -E "^import .* from 'node:[a-z]+';$", which saw the five lines server.ts has today only because of how it spells them. A harmless respelling made the set incomplete and reddened four cells while server.ts still worked.
The whole change is one file. The grep is replaced by a small extractor, extract_node_imports, that reads the import statement (either quote style, optional semicolon, a clause wrapped over lines, a trailing comment, CRLF, any node: specifier including node:child_process and node:fs/promises) and prints each in one canonical spelling. On the real server.ts it prints exactly what the old grep printed: five identical lines. server.ts is never edited (blob 306f8a1a4b5f before and after). .dockerignore:14 is **/__tests__, so the file reaches no image.
Twelve cells are added, and the suite goes from 8/0 to 20/0. The extractor is written into the fixture directory and used for the real subject and for eight synthetic spellings, a subpath/underscore case and three controls, so what is tested is what is used.

70.1 Respelling is harmless; deleting an import is not

The control that matters is kept and still fires. The existing cell that the inherited set is non-empty and names node:path and node:url is unchanged. Under the new suite it is red on all three deletion arms (the path import deleted, the url import deleted, all five deleted) and green on every respelling. The four cells the old grep wrongly reddened on a respelling are the same four that go red on a real deletion, so the suite did not lose a signal; it stopped raising a false one.
The old grep only reds when the missing import is one the expression needs. A trailing comment on the fs import left the old suite green at 8/0 (the expression does not use fs), while the same comment on the path import reddened it. That asymmetry is why a respelling can sit unnoticed until it lands on a needed line.

m2 adds seven cells: a fixture .env that carries GATEWAY_PORT=9999 and WEBSITE_PORT=9998, and an assertion that slot 2’s banner still names 6982 and 6981 (and the unslotted run the historic 6882 and 6881). m1 changes the checker (+27/−6): the website-origin check now walks every comma-separated origin list in MUST_MOVE (api-gateway and demo-service; auth.FRONTEND_URL is a single URL and has no website half), and api-gateway’s coverage is kept as a named assertion so a change to its default cannot quietly drop it out of the loop. 73.1 Why the m1 cells need no Docker

A stub docker on PATH and a canned render. The checker needs the docker compose CLI but not a daemon: config only parses. It resolves docker from PATH and consumes only config --format json, so the REAL .mjs and the REAL stack_env.sh run in a fixture repo while the stub answers compose version and prints a canned render. The render models only what the checker reads: ownership labels, published ports, project and container names, the three MUST_MOVE values and the six KNOWN_SLOT_BLIND ones. It is not the real compose file, so these cells prove the checker’s logic and say nothing about what docker-compose.yml renders.
A control makes the canned render trustworthy: with every website half moved the checker is green (rc=0, OK —) and the stub logged exactly the bare, slot 1 and slot 2 renders, so a red below is attributable to the one reverted half. A second control keeps api-gateway’s own check honest: reverting its website half still fails the checker and names it.

74. The document-lookup catch can no longer be taken down by its own log line, and a thrown null is pinned (KS-1524)

What this changes. KS-1524 collects the residue the KS 1510 gate left on GET /api/platform/document-lookup. This change takes items (c) and (a). Item (b), the exact-message pin (cell L5), was already merged by PR 1699. Items (d), cap the logged line, and (e), a measurement on the live ingress, are held: one is a decision and the other needs a deploy.
(c), a thrown null. typeof null is 'object', so the err !== null in the log expression is the only thing keeping Object.getPrototypeOf(null) from throwing inside the catch. Cell L6 throws null and asserts the constant 500 and the line thrown object. The gate’s mutant O11 (that guard removed) left every cell green; it now fails L6 alone.
(a), a behaviour change on a request path. Building the log line, and writing it, were both unguarded inside the catch. A thrown value that cannot be described (a message getter that throws, a Proxy whose getPrototypeOf or ownKeys trap throws, a revoked Proxy) or a logger that throws made the async handler reject from its own catch, and the request got no response. The value is now described in its own try (fallback line thrown value that could not be described) and logged in another, so the constant 500 is always sent. For every value that could be described before, the line is unchanged.

75. get_info keeps its notes honest at the edges: two survivor cells, the status wording and its comment (KS-1620)

What this fixes. secuura_get_connector_info (Blockchain/Dev/services/mcp-server/src/tools/info.ts) turns the gateway’s answer into a note. Gate D left three follow-ups; item 1, the 200-character bound, is already on develop with its own cells B1 to B4. This change is items 2 and 3. Two mutants survived the whole suite: H1-M3, dropping !connectorResult.ok, made a 200 whose body is null read “refused by the gateway (200)”; H1-M8, loosening typeof ...message === 'string' to != null, sent the number 123 into .slice so the tool answered with an error object instead of a note. A code comment also called every status but 401/404 a deliberate refusal.
Five cells are added to the ks1620 test (4 to 9): H1-M3 (a 200 with a JSON null body keeps the not-available note), H1-M8 (a non-string message relays no text), and one cell each for 400, 429 and 502, statuses no other cell drives, asserting the note still reads “Connector info refused by the gateway (<status>)”. Item 2 took the ticket’s second option, as ruled for this lane on 2026-10-27: keep the word “refused” and correct the comment. The comment at info.ts:129 is one line replaced by one line (173 lines before and after): it now says that a 403/503 fail-closed is a deliberate refusal and a 400, 429, 500 or proxy 502 is not, and that the status in the note is how a reader tells them apart. No code line changes.

75.1 What a cell can pin, and the comment-only proof

The sentence cannot be pinned; the behaviour it describes can. No cell can fail because a comment is worded badly. The new 400, 429 and 502 cells pin what the comment describes, the kept wording and the status carried in the note; the existing C3 cell in the ks1541 test still pins 500. Changing the user-visible wording was not taken.

77. countUsers answers a database fault like listUsers, so a faulting count is a 503 and not a raw 500 (KS-1769)

What this fixes. Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/repositories/userRepo.ts: countUsersInner had no try/catch, so a database fault in the COUNT answered a raw 500 (INTERNAL_ERROR) on GET /api/users and GET /api/users/admin/list. Both routes call listUsers and then countUsers on one request, and listUsers has answered 503 since KS 1484, so with the list answering and the count faulting the route still came back 500. countUsersInner now carries a spelled-out copy of the list’s catch: the query and the parse are inside the try; an infrastructure fault (isInfrastructureDbError) becomes ServiceUnavailableError (503, SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE); anything else is rethrown as the very same error; the failure is logged as DB countUsers failed with the error and its code. The WHERE builder stays outside the try. A behaviour change on the user-listing path.
Twelve cells are appended to services/auth/src/__tests__/ks1186-userrepo-fromrow-sites-are-awaited.test.ts (23 → 35): four red-first, three controls on the result path (a non-infrastructure fault is the very same error, a clean count returns the number and logs nothing, an empty result counts 0), and five controls that the filters still reach the query as the same SQL and the same bound values.
The two search clauses in those filter controls pin today’s ILIKE text. KS 1168 (the encrypted-column search) rewrites them on purpose and has to update those cells in the same change.

78. Five originate log-line describers can no longer take a request down: the fail500 helpers of four route files and the per-tenant catch of migrate-tenant-data (KS-1772)

What this changes. KS-1772 names five places in services/originate where a log line was built from a thrown value with no try of its own, the shape PR 1754 fixed in api-gateway (KS-1524 (a)). The five are the fail500 helper of routes/systemErrors.ts, routes/gdpr.ts, routes/webhooks.ts and routes/adminConfig.ts, and the per-tenant catch of POST /api/admin/migrate-tenant-data in adminConfig.ts.
A behaviour change on request paths. A thrown value whose description throws (a message getter that throws, a Proxy whose getPrototypeOf or ownKeys trap throws, a revoked Proxy), or a logger that throws, made the describer throw from inside its own catch. In the four fail500 helpers that rejected the async handler, Express 4 never sees a rejected promise, and the request got no response. In the per-tenant catch it escaped into the route’s outer catch: the loop stopped at that tenant, later tenants were never tried, and the route answered 500 where its contract is a 200 whose results carries the failing tenant’s code.
Each site now describes the value in its own try (fallback line thrown value that could not be described) and logs in another, so the constant 500, or the tenant’s row and the next tenant, is always produced. For every value that could be described before, the log line is unchanged. The guards are written inline at each site and not as a shared helper: the per-tenant row TENANT_COPY_FAILED, its bare-string shape and a shared describer are KS-1462 item 2, and are not touched.

78.1 Scope: four route files, one new test file

Five non-test hunks in four files. adminConfig.ts (two hunks, 31 lines added and 5 removed), and gdpr.ts, systemErrors.ts and webhooks.ts (14 added and 1 removed each). The describing expression is byte-identical: its exact text occurs 5 times at base and 5 times after (2 in adminConfig.ts, 1 in each of the others), and a control with one character of it altered finds 0.
The new test is services/originate/src/__tests__/ks1772-originate-log-line-describers-cannot-hang-a-request.test.ts: 30 cells over the five sites, each driving the real route on a loopback listener. Per site there are four D1 cells (one per throwing shape), one L1 cell (a logger that throws on a value that describes fine) and one C1 control (a describable Error is logged by its message, so the stub is live and a green D1 or L1 is not vacuous).
Not guarded here. The api-gateway half of the same pattern, six sites, is KS-1771. The read-only controls ks1346a to ks1346d and ks730c are not edited.

78.3 What the cells prove, and what they do not

The route’s answer, not the process. The cells prove that each route answers (and the per-tenant catch goes on to the next tenant) for the four throwing shapes and for a throwing logger, over a loopback listener with the service calls mocked. They do not say what an unhandled rejection does to a running service: that is the process’s unhandledRejection posture, a separate ticket (KS-1427).
The catch around each logger.error is deliberately empty, with its reason written beside it: if the logger itself fails there is no other channel to report it on, and the caller must still get its answer. This is a named exception, not a silenced error.
Not measured: any of this through a running gateway or on a deployed box, a run on Node 24, and the four platform suites (Schemathesis, Akto, Playwright, Performance/k6), which are not claimed as passing. Two existing ESLint warnings in adminConfig.ts (prefer-const on copied, and an unused e) are present at base and are not touched.

AUTH_GREEN_SUMMARY is now a RegExp that refuses a digit directly before 0 new; runsComparedAsOneValue bounds a compared value by the bracket that closes the one the argument opened; two new cells pin every ordinary expectRun call and a floor on their number. 79.1 Item 3: the green summary is a RegExp, and the line it must match was captured, not composed

The line, the worse lines, and what was left alone. The file counts in it will drift, and the cell does not compare it to a live run.

79.2 Item 1: the guard counts depth, and steps over strings

The depth scan. runsComparedAsOneValue found an expect( argument opened by [ or { and read to the first ] or }. It now reads to the bracket that closes the one the argument opened, found by counting depth, so an index ahead of .status, an index ahead of .out, the object form with an index ahead of the second field, an index inside an index and an array of arrays are all seen. A value that never closes is scanned to the end of the text, as before.
Counting depth would read across the end of the value on a bracket inside a string, a false-positive class the old bound did not have. The scan steps over single-quoted, double-quoted and template-literal strings and honours a backslash. Eight forbidden and four permitted rows are added to the tables of shapes planted in a copy of the file; a quoted bracket and a template-literal bracket followed by a use of both fields are permitted shapes.
Not covered: a comment or a regular-expression literal inside the compared value that holds a quote or a bracket. The ticket’s open question, searched: neither the old regex nor the new scan finds the shape in any of the 105 test files under services/auth, nor in the 621 under services or the 54 under packages. The planted nested index is missed by the old regex and found by the new one, and the edited file itself returns nothing.

79.3 Item 2: measured first, then pinned

What the measurement showed, and how far the pin goes. The syntax tree holds 39 expectRun calls; the textual count of 43 also counts the definition, a doc comment and two mutant strings. Nine sit inside expect(() => ...) or thrownBy(() => ...) and are the subject of cells that expect them to throw. 30 are ordinary call sites.
Each call’s predicate was dropped, one at a time, in a sibling copy of the file with the status check kept, and the enclosing cell was run alone. Of the 29 ordinary calls other than the REAL cell’s, 29 stayed green. The REAL call stays green alone and is killed by the KS-1529 pin cell, so it was the only protected one. Of the nine calls under test, six were killed and three stayed green. Controls: an unmutated copy passed, and a copy with one call replaced by a failing assertion went red.
The pin: every ordinary call keeps a numeric status and a predicate that can fail (not '', not a RegExp that matches everything), and the file keeps at least 30 ordinary calls, so a call replaced by a bare status check, or removed, is counted. A call that lost the predicate argument altogether is also a TS2554 under the test-types ratchet.
Not proved: that any predicate is the RIGHT one; a predicate swapped for another that can fail; a removal paired with an addition elsewhere (measured: one call replaced by a bare status check and one added, and the cells stay green); a predicate held in a name or a template, which is taken as present; the nine calls under test. A table of counts keyed by cell title would close the swap case.

Their handlers are async and Express 4 does not catch the rejection. The gateway survives unhandled rejections on purpose (KS 546), so the request is simply never answered. The 20 unhandled rejections are these four sites times five inputs.
A different answer, 5 of 5 each: the 502 catch in audit-export.ts falls to the handler’s outer catch, so fail500 answers 500 under another log context instead of the 502. In notifications.ts the six handlers are synchronous, so the throw reaches Express and the gateway’s errorHandler answers in place of the route’s constant 500.

80.3 What the cells prove, and what they do not

The route’s answer, not the process. The cells prove each route sends its constant answer for those five inputs and logs the fallback line; at the audit-log catch the answer is the degraded 200 (the audit_logs row, the platform half dropped). They do not say what an unhandled rejection does to a running gateway.
The empty catch is deliberate. The catch around each log call is empty, with its reason written beside it: if the logger itself fails there is no other channel to report it on, and the caller must still get its answer. It is a named exception, not a silenced error.
One injection caveat. The audit-log catch is driven through the response-body read (await r.json()), because fetchWithTimeout evaluates err instanceof Error in its own catch and would replace two of the four hostile shapes with a plain TypeError before they reached the catch under test.

81. api-client.ts declares the error body the gateway sends: a string or an object { code, message } at all three sites (KS-1767)

What this changes. KS-1767 records that the MCP server’s api-client.ts typed a response’s error as a string at three sites (registerDocument, getWorkflowInstance, getConnectorInfo) while the gateway’s published error body carries an object { code, message }. Nothing was failing: nothing checks the declared type at run time, because apiRequest only casts the parsed body to it. The type said one thing and the wire said another, and a caller that trusted it could relay [object Object] or the whole object.
A type-only change. The three declarations now use one alias, GatewayErrorField = string | { code?: string; message?: string }, and the as unknown as cast in tools/info.ts that worked round the old type is dropped. The emitted JavaScript of info.ts (comments removed) is identical, line for line, so no behaviour changes.
details, optional in the published ErrorResponse, is not declared because no caller reads it. Three other places read data.error and relay it into a JSON error field (tools/info.ts for the workflow instance, and tools/register.ts twice). They are not changed: they compile under either type, and whether they should relay an object is a behaviour question this ticket does not ask.

82. GET /api/anchors/:documentId answers 500, not 404, when its database read fails (KS-1657)

What this changes. KS-1657: getAnchorByDocumentId in originate’s routes/anchors.ts caught every error and returned null, and its only caller, the GET /:documentId handler, reads null as “no anchor on record” and answers 404 with anchored: false. A failed read and a genuine absence were one answer. The catch now logs the same warn line and rethrows, so a fault reaches the route’s own catch and answers its constant 500 INTERNAL_ERROR; zero rows is still the same 404 body. Kam’s ruling, 2026-10-28 07:13 AEDT: “a — Fix it”.
One source file changes: throw err replaces return null in the catch, with a three-line comment naming the ticket and the prior behaviour. The new test is services/originate/src/__tests__/ks1657-an-anchor-read-fault-is-not-a-404.test.ts (8 cells). No tier timing or budget in these documents moves.

82.1 Why 500 and not 503

There is no classifier in originate to reuse. auth classifies infrastructure faults with isInfrastructureDbError (services/auth/src/repositories/dbErrors.ts), which reads pg error codes (classes 08, 53, 57), socket error codes and pg pool messages. originate reads through Prisma (prisma.$queryRaw), whose errors carry other codes and other text, and a search of services/originate/src outside the tests finds no classifier and no service-unavailable error type (the 503 hits are OpenAPI declarations and the load-shedding mount in index.ts). A 503 here would mean writing and proving a new classifier for one route. The route’s existing catch already answers a constant 500, which is inside Kam’s ruling (“500/503”), and the coordinator accepted it: do not import auth’s helper across services for this.
The other shape the ticket names, a discriminated result, was not chosen: it would carry one bit (fault or absence) through a single caller that already has a catch. Letting the error propagate changes one line and leaves null meaning one thing only.

83. GET /api/platform/document-lookup is in the published contract, as a public route (KS-1773)

What this changes. KS-1773: the handler (routes/platform.ts line 1106) was live and absent from the published spec, so the contract said nothing about an anonymous caller, who gets a 400 when no parameter is sent and not a 401. Kam’s ruling, 2026-10-28 07:14 AEDT: “a — Keep it public and publish it”. The operation is now registered in api-gateway.openapi.ts and the regenerated docs/openapi/secuura-api.yaml gains it (119 lines added, none removed: one path and two schemas). It declares security: [], the query parameters hash and documentId, and the answers 200, 400, 429, 500 and 503. There is no 404: a lookup that matches nothing is a 200 with an empty results list.
No handler change. The new test is services/api-gateway/src/__tests__/ks1773-document-lookup-is-in-the-published-contract.test.ts (vitest, 18 cells). No tier timing or budget in these documents moves.

83.1 What publishing changes at runtime

Documenting a path is not inert. The gateway reads the yaml at boot (index.ts line 612) and answers 405 with Allow: GET to any method the spec does not declare on a documented path (index.ts lines 1064 to 1081). After a deploy and a gateway restart (the yaml is bind-mounted locally and baked into the image on a deployed target), every non-GET method on this path, HEAD included, is a 405 with Allow: GET. POST, PUT and DELETE were the fall-through 404; HEAD was answered by the GET handler. The coordinator accepted this as a direct consequence of “publish it”. Cell R1 pins it for POST, DELETE and HEAD.
It does not move authentication. The operation declares no bearerAuth, and specRouteMap.ts line 47 arms the edge auth gate for bearerAuth only, so an anonymous GET still reaches the handler and gets its own 400. Cells U2 and R2 pin that; declaring bearerAuth reds both.

83.2 Where each answer comes from

Read from the handler and the init DDL, with line numbers in the comment above the registration. 400: neither hash nor documentId, an empty value counting as absent (platform.ts 1110 to 1111). 503: PLATFORM_DATABASE_URL unset (1114 to 1116). 200: { success: true, results: [...] }, up to five rows, seven fields (1125 to 1148); hash is tested first, so documentId is ignored when both are sent. 500: any other failure, a constant body (1152 to 1170).
429 is the gateway’s global per-minute limiter (index.ts line 479); this path is not in its exempt list (middleware/rateLimitSkip.ts line 23), so it applies here as to every other /api route. It is not the handler’s answer and is not exercised by cells W1 to W8.
Column types are read from the init DDL (docker/init-platform/01-platform-schema.sql lines 209 to 221): tenant_slug, document_type, title, status and certified_at are nullable there, so they are nullable in the schema. The live platform database was not queried.

85. isPlatformRole and requireKeyAdmin compare the role as an exact ASCII fold and refuse a role that is not a string (KS-1591)

What this changes. KS-1591 (a security nit, pre-existing): two predicates decided “platform administrator” and “key administrator” with String(role).toUpperCase(), which is not an identity test. U+0131 (dotless i) upper-cases to I, U+017F (long s) upper-cases to S, and a role ARRAY stringifies to its element, so a role spelled with either character, or an array holding SUPER_ADMIN, read as an admin role. isPlatformRole in packages/shared/src/security/keyRevokePolicy.ts and requireKeyAdmin in services/security/src/index.ts now apply an ASCII fold only (a-z to A-Z, every other character untouched) and treat a role that is not a string as no role. 88. The IPFS service bounds all eight of its outbound fetches, and a gateway body that stalls answers 503 (KS-1240 part 3)

What this changes. KS-1240 part 3, services/nft-certificate/src/services/ipfs.service.ts: eight outbound fetch calls (Pinata upload, pin and unpin; Infura add, pin/add and pin/rm; Web3.Storage upload; the gateway read in IPFSService.fetch) carried no timeout, so a provider or gateway that accepted the connection and then went quiet held the caller for as long as the socket lived. Each call now passes AbortSignal.timeout: 60 s for the three uploads, 15 s for the four pin and unpin calls, 30 s for the gateway read. On expiry the handling each call already had answers: an upload returns { success: false }, pin and unpin return false, the gateway read throws ServiceUnavailableError (503).
The gateway body read moved inside a try. response.arrayBuffer() sat outside the try that maps a failed connect to 503, so a gateway that sent its headers and then stalled the body, or dropped the connection part-way through it, surfaced as the raw error (TimeoutError or TypeError: terminated, neither carrying a status) and not as the 503 the method’s own comment promises. The read now maps any body failure to the same 503 and logs IPFS gateway body read failed.
Scope, and a trade-off. The ticket text names only the api-gateway key-validate fetch; this part was added by the coordinator’s brief, not by the ticket. An object the gateway needs more than 30 s to deliver now answers 503 where it used to wait.

88.1 What each call did before the fix

Measured at base bd6697e079fc, 2026-10-28 (UTC), Kamil’s MacBook Pro (Mac14,5, Apple M2 Max, 32 GB), shared with other sessions. The new test file (15 cells: five gateway-read cells over a real local http server, seven provider cells over a stubbed fetch that honours init.signal, one bounds cell, one source scan and one scanner control) against the UNFIXED service: 12 failed / 3 passed, the three passes being the controls.
The gateway read. A gateway that accepts the connection and sends nothing, and one that sends its headers and a first chunk and then stalls, never answer (the cell reports hung after 2 s). A gateway that drops the connection part-way through the body rejects with TypeError: terminated and no status.
The seven provider calls each hang against an endpoint that never answers, and the source scan lists all eight call sites as unbounded (lines 70, 105, 123, 166, 195, 208, 239 and 463).

89. The published OAuth authorize contract names the OAuth token and the role-or-scope door (KS-1472)

What this changes. KS-1472: the sentence in both /api/oauth/authorize descriptions (GET and POST) read “A token with no scopes satisfies no scope requirement, so a route that requires a scope refuses it (403); a route that requires none accepts any valid token.” It now reads “An OAuth token with no scopes satisfies no scope requirement, so a route that requires a scope refuses it (403), unless the route also admits the caller by role; a route that requires no scope does not refuse it for want of one, though a role check on that route can still refuse it.” The ticket’s three points: (1) a plain login JWT with no scopes passes requireScope on RBAC (the jwt and email branch in middleware/scopes.ts), so only an OAuth token is refused; (2) requireOrgProvisioner (routes/platform.ts) admits SUPER_ROLES by role with no scope; (3) “requires none” read as none of anything, while role, MFA and tenant gates can still refuse.
QA gate round 1 (GO WITH NOTES) on the first published wording, which ended “a route that requires no scope accepts any valid token.”: that clause is false for a route with a role gate. requireSuperAdmin (api-gateway routes/platform.ts, lines 67 to 74) answers 403 on a role outside SUPER_ROLES, and GET /api/platform/tenants runs authenticateToken() then requireSuperAdmin with no requireScope (the file has none). The clause is narrowed to the sentence above: the route does not refuse for want of a scope, and a role check on it can still refuse. Only the role check is named, because it is the one that was read; the MFA and tenant gates the ticket also mentioned were not read and are not claimed. The first published wording, in full: “An OAuth token with no scopes satisfies no scope requirement, so a route that requires a scope refuses it (403), unless the route also admits the caller by role; a route that requires no scope accepts any valid token.”
The wording is edited in services/auth/src/auth.openapi.ts only; docs/openapi/secuura-api.yaml is regenerated, never hand-edited. The ks839 pin STATES_THE_TOKEN and its header moved to the new wording. Point 4 of the ticket (the guard cell forbids one exact wording of the false claim) is left, as the ticket says. Point 5: the ks1210 header said its control checks name too; it reads redirectUris only, so the header sentence was corrected and no toContain('name') check was added, because a bare substring check passes on any text that contains “name” and would claim more than it proves.

92. The Blockchain/Testing entry points aim at the slot that was named, and refuse to guess (KS-1382)

What this changes. KS-1382: the five Internal Audit Harness entry points (ci/orchestrate.sh, ci/tools/run-schemathesis.sh, jobs/05-dast-zap.sh, jobs/06-tenant-isolation.sh, run-internal-audit.sh) and tests/tenant-isolation/runner.ts used to default TARGET_BASE to slot 1’s gateway, the historic port, when it was not passed. On a slot-N worktree, forgetting the variable aimed ZAP, the tenant-isolation probes and the audit at whichever stack owned slot 1, usually another session’s: the KS-1373 failure shape, in the shell harness. They now take the target from the slot that was named (SECUURA_STACK_SLOT, or the platform-s alias STACK_SLOT), read from Blockchain/Dev/scripts/stack_env.sh. Nothing in the tree types a port.
Authority. The ticket’s Fix section spells the shape out. Seven choices it leaves open (how a slot counts as named, how the port is read, what “disagree” means, the refusal text, where the static guard lives, one inline block versus a helper file, and runner.ts) were ruled by Wednesday: “[Wednesday -> Secuura/Blockchain-Z] ANSWER: plan confirmation (Seat Z 3rd) - GO, D1-D7 ruled”, 2026-10-28 06:32:34Z.
Section number. This block is section 92, set at the merge as develop’s highest plus one. It was drafted under an earlier number at base bd6697e079fc.

92.1 What each combination does

One block, byte for byte, in all five scripts (a suite cell pins them equal). No TARGET_BASE, a slot named: that slot’s gateway, read from stack_env.sh in a subshell so nothing it exports reaches the script or its docker jobs.
No TARGET_BASE, no slot: refused with rc 2 and the example command, in KS-1016’s wording. It never falls back to any slot.
TARGET_BASE, no slot: used unchanged. This is the CI path. It is looser than KS-1016’s rule for the harnesses, because CI passes the variable and names no slot, and two existing suites (ks1405, orchestrate_jobs) run the scripts the same way.
TARGET_BASE and a slot: used unchanged, unless it is a LOCAL url on ANOTHER slot’s gateway, which is refused (the KS-1373 split-target shape). A remote host, or a local port that is no slot’s gateway (a stub), is left alone.
SECUURA_TARGET_RESOLVE_ONLY=1 prints the resolved TARGET_BASE and exits 0 before any job, curl, docker or tsx starts. None of the scripts had such a mode; it is the suite’s seam.

92.2 The static guard

check-stack-safety.sh section 3d extends the slot-derivation group’s single guard (3c) over Blockchain/Testing. A published port of any slot, typed as a standalone number in a tracked file under Blockchain/Testing, fails. The port set is derived from stack_env.sh under env -i (48 numbers across slots 1 to 4), never typed. The pattern matches a bare number, not only :PORT, so copying the port arithmetic with slot 1’s number typed is caught; a number that merely contains a port, or sits in a version, is not.
Four exceptions, each with a reason and a ticket, each excusing a real hit (an exception that excuses nothing fails as stale): the USER SIMULATED TEST run records, the baselines, the reconfirm-5xx URL fixtures, and the CI snippet (KS-1162). The guard reads green on the tree: 110 invariants hold.

93. The api-gateway front door answers 503 when an API key cannot be checked, and every hand-built gateway fetch is bounded (KS-1240)

What this changes. KS-1240: the two front-door calls in middleware/auth.ts (key validation at the security service, the connector-token exchange at auth) and nine hand-built forwards (routes/proxy.ts five, routes/admin.ts two, routes/batch.ts one, routes/audit-export.ts one) carried no timeout, so an upstream that never answered, or answered the headers and stalled the body, held the request open with no bound. And the front door could not tell “this key is rejected” from “I could not ask”: a thrown fetch answered 401 Invalid API key, and the security service’s own 503 'Unable to verify key' was answered 401 and negative-cached for 30 s.
Five source files change and two test files are new: services/api-gateway/src/__tests__/ks1240b-front-door-key-exchange-timeout-answers-503-not-401.test.ts (12 cells) and services/api-gateway/src/__tests__/ks1240b-every-hand-built-gateway-fetch-is-bounded.test.ts (28 cells), both vitest. No tier timing or budget in these documents moves.

93.1 What a client sees now

A presented sk_ key. checkApiKey returns valid, rejected or unavailable. Unavailable is no complete answer within 5 s (a hang or a stalled body), an unreadable body, or a 5xx, 408 or 429 from the security service. It answers 503 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE 'Unable to verify API key, please retry' on required AND optional mounts, is never cached, and is logged once as API_KEY_VALIDATION_UNAVAILABLE with its reason and never the key. Authority: Kam’s rulings on cards secuura-ks888-revoke-validate-on-failed-save (a) and secuura-ks1370-validate-when-the-revoke-check-cannot-read (a), that an unverifiable key is refused with 503.
Rejected keeps every answer it had: 401 Invalid API key and a 30 s negative cache on a required mount, and the KS-1207 fall-through to the Bearer path on an optional mount. A non-2xx with no status that says “could not answer” (any 4xx other than 408 and 429, or no status at all) is still a rejection, as auth.test.ts pins.
Optional mounts answer 503 for an unverifiable key instead of serving the caller as anonymous: the caller asked to be the key’s principal. It is a refusal, never a pass, so KS-1207’s guarantee (a junk key cannot switch off the Bearer check) holds.
The exchange stays fail-closed: within 5 s the request goes on with no Bearer, and a Bearer-only upstream refuses it 401, as before; the log now says “timed out after 5000 ms”. The ticket’s line that a 503 “is consistent with how the connector branch already answers a refused exchange” was checked and is not borne out: no gateway code answers a refused exchange with 503, and auth’s /internal/connector-token answers 502. A gateway 503 there would also refuse the gateway-local handlers that serve sk_ callers from req.user without the Bearer.

93.2 The bounds, and what the forwards now answer

Two values, each a named constant. 5 s for the two front-door calls (KEY_VALIDATE_TIMEOUT_MS, CONNECTOR_EXCHANGE_TIMEOUT_MS): the bound the gateway’s own health probes give the same internal services. 60 s for every hand-built forward (UPSTREAM_FORWARD_TIMEOUT_MS in proxy.ts and admin.ts, BATCH_ITEM_TIMEOUT_MS, AUDIT_LIST_TIMEOUT_MS): the generic proxy’s proxyTimeout for every other route to the same upstreams, so hand-building a route neither tightens nor loosens it. MCP package generation takes 60 s too: the package is built from templates in-process.
The signal on the fetch also bounds the body read that follows it. Measured on Node 26.8.1 with a probe outside the repo: a hang before the headers, and a stall in the middle of json(), text() or arrayBuffer(), each reject with DOMException TimeoutError at the bound; a refused connection is TypeError: fetch failed.
A body cut off by the timeout now reaches each route’s own catch (502, like a connect failure) instead of reading as {} with the upstream’s status; a body that is simply not JSON still reads as {}. A batch item whose body never arrived now FAILS (“Upstream service did not answer in time”); it used to be a success with empty data. generate-package reads the whole package before it writes Content-Type: application/zip and the attachment disposition, which it used to write first, so a failed read sent the 502 as a zip attachment. The arrayBuffer() read itself was already inside the route’s try at the base; the header order was the defect.

94. A social sign-in provider that does not answer in time is classified as unavailable, and every provider fetch is bounded (KS-1240)

What this changes. KS-1240: the six social provider adapters in services/auth/src/providers/social/ (GitHub, Google, LinkedIn, Apple, Facebook, Microsoft) made 12 fetches with no timeout, so a provider that never answered, or answered the headers and stalled the body, held the sign-in request open with no bound, on the login callback and on POST /social/link alike.
The six adapters change and one test file is new: services/auth/src/__tests__/ks1240b-social-provider-fetches-are-bounded-and-classified.test.ts (vitest, 44 cells). routes/auth.ts and middleware/errorHandler.ts are unchanged. No tier timing or budget in these documents moves.

94.1 What each entry path answers now

A timeout, or a provider that cannot be reached, is the provider being unavailable. Each adapter carries one 10 s constant (PROVIDER_TIMEOUT_MS) and one small helper. Every fetch has AbortSignal.timeout, which also bounds the body read after it, and exchangeCode turns only a timeout into the existing ServiceUnavailableError (KS-253, 503 SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE) with the text “<Provider> did not answer in time; please try again.” It is thrown from the adapter, so neither route file changes.
POST /social/link has no local try, so the error handler answers it 503; before, the request hung. The login callback wraps every exchange failure in its own BadRequestError, so it still answers 400, now as “OAuth authentication failed: GitHub did not answer in time; please try again.” instead of hanging. Its OAuth state is consumed before the exchange, as before, so a timed-out sign-in needs a fresh one.
A refused or unresolvable provider (fetch’s own TypeError: fetch failed) is classified the same way, with the text “<Provider> could not be reached; please try again.”: 503 on /social/link (was 500) and the classified 400 on the callback. A TypeError that is not a network failure stays unclassified.
The provider’s own error text no longer reaches the client (gate 5, finding 1788-1). Every adapter put await tokenRes.text() into its token-refusal Error, and the callback echoed it (the gate measured a JSON error_description and an upstream HTML page). The Error now carries the status only, “<Provider> token exchange failed (HTTP 400)”, and the provider text is logged server-side, first 200 characters, as routes/auth.ts bounds error_description. A token 4xx or 5xx is still not classified as unavailable (500 on the link route), and a profile call answered 401 still rejects with its adapter’s own error. The cells assert status, code and message, never instanceof ServiceUnavailableError: at this base AppError’s constructor resets every subclass instance to AppError.prototype (KS-1467 in auth), and only instanceof AppError, which the error handler uses, holds.

95. Tenant creation bounds its two outbound fetches: a hung tokenisation or security service ends in the fail-soft path an unreachable one already took (KS-1240 part 4)

What this changes. KS-1240 part 4, services/tenant-provisioning: POST /api/tenants made two outbound fetches with no timeout, the vault key generation to the tokenisation service (requestKeyGeneration in index.ts) and the metering-key mint to the security service (requestMeteringKey in meteringKey.ts). Each now passes AbortSignal.timeout with a named 3 s bound (KEY_GENERATION_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS, METERING_KEY_FETCH_TIMEOUT_MS). On expiry the fetch (or the body read) rejects into the try/catch each call already sat in, the same path an unreachable service takes.
Only the bounds change. The status and the body of every path are exactly what they were, and so are the writes of an unreachable or a hung service, with one exception: a service that is merely SLOWER than the bound (not hung). Where the unbounded code waited and returned the key (and so did the first 10 s version of this change, for an answer between 3 s and 10 s), the bounded code answers 201 with keyFile (or meteringApiKey) null in the body and stores vault_key_hash as NULL, while the key service still completes its own insert (exercised in the vault-key trace); nothing reads either value. What the route SHOULD answer when key generation cannot complete (today a 201 with keyFile: null and an empty vault_key_hash) is a separate decision and is not made here: it was decided on 2026-10-28 (option b, an explicit key-pending flag) and is built as a separate PR after this one.
Scope. The ticket text names only the api-gateway key-validate fetch; this part was added by the coordinator’s brief, not by the ticket.

95.1 What tenant creation did before the fix, and answers today

Measured at base bd6697e079fc, 2026-10-28 (UTC), Kamil’s MacBook Pro (Mac14,5, Apple M2 Max, 32 GB), shared with other sessions. The real service entry module, with pg replaced by a recorder and the JWT middleware by a pass-through, against real local servers that answer, stall or are shut down. The “DB row” is the parameters the route sends to the recorder, not a row in a database.
A hung tokenisation service, unbounded: the request never answers, and the only write is the tenant INSERT with status provisioning. No tenant_config, no status update, no audit row and no rollback follow (the rollback runs only on a throw), 3 s and 1 s later: a half-created tenant. A hung security service, unbounded: the tenant IS fully written and active (four writes) and the request still never answers, because the mint is the last step.
Bounded, a hung service and an unreachable one end identically: 201, success: true, tenant active, keyFile: null (tokenisation) or meteringApiKey: null (security), vault_key_hash stored as NULL when key generation failed, the same four writes. Only the log line differs (fetch failed against The operation was aborted due to timeout).
A third path nobody logs: a tokenisation service that answers 403 { success: false } ends in the same 201 with keyFile: null and a NULL hash, and writes no log line at all (unchanged by this change).

95.3 What the cells prove, and what they do not

The bound and the unchanged answer, not production timings. The route cells shorten the bound to 150 ms by wrapping AbortSignal.timeout; the cell that pins the length asks for exactly two 3 s bounds. The front door. The only gateway route to this handler, POST /api/platform/tenants (services/api-gateway/src/routes/platform.ts: the deadline is declared at line 132 and the route is registered from line 314, at develop d531abd5f34b), forwards with a default deadline of PLATFORM_UPSTREAM_TIMEOUT_MS, 8000 ms, and answers 504 when it expires (read from the code, not measured through a real gateway). The two bounds run one after the other, so with both services hung the create takes about 6 s plus the route’s own writes. A 10 s bound, the first choice, never fired first: the gateway answered 504 at 8 s while tenant creation finished afterwards and minted a metering key nobody received (tier 1 gate round 1, finding 1782-1). The generic proxy’s own timeout (routes/proxy.ts) is not the one this route uses. One cell runs the create with both services hung at the real bounds: a 201 after 6068 ms, five runs, against the 8000 ms deadline. The 1500 ms allowance for the writes inside the remaining margin is a stated allowance, not a measurement, and the deadline is a default an operator can change with the environment variable. A service that is slower than 3 s but not hung now takes the fail-soft path where the first version waited up to 10 s.
Not covered. A real tokenisation or security service; a real database row; Docker; the 409 a retry would meet after an unbounded hang (read from index.ts lines 206 to 213, not measured); Node 24; the four platform suites (Schemathesis, Akto, Playwright, Performance/k6). The change is not deployed.
Any change to what the route answers (a pending flag, a refusal) would change the published 201 contract (tenant-provisioning.openapi.ts and the OpenAPI yaml) and is held for a ruling.

98. The m365 callback’s success redirect encodes the connection id, as it already encodes the tenant (KS-1670, site 1)

What this changes. 100. Two originate catches can no longer be hung by a hostile thrown value: the system-errors list and extractPgCode (KS-1780, part 1 and part 3)

What this changes. KS-1780 (originate): several catches read the thrown value before they reach fail500. A revoked Proxy, a Proxy whose getPrototypeOf trap throws, or an object whose getter throws makes that read throw from inside the catch, so the handler’s promise rejects and the request gets no response at all (the KS-1772 shape, one step earlier). This change closes two of the sites. In routes/systemErrors.ts the list route’s err instanceof z.ZodError becomes a new local isZodError(err), which returns false for a value that cannot be inspected. In utils/pgErrors.ts extractPgCode now wraps its reads of code, meta.code and message in a try and returns undefined if they throw (the old body is unchanged, renamed readPgCode); the PATCH /api/webhooks/:id catch calls it before fail500, and webhooks.ts itself is not edited. A value that cannot be read is not a ZodError and has no code, so the handler answers its constant 500. Two local-model passes (the Spark, DeepSeek V4 Flash: ks_1780_p1 and ks_1780_p3_webhooks) each passed their checker 7 of 7 and are byte-identical to the drafter’s golden; both were applied here strictly and unchanged.
systemErrors.ts changes +13 / −1 and pgErrors.ts +10 / −0; the two files share no line. The new tests are ks1780-system-errors-list-catch-cannot-hang-on-a-hostile-throw.test.ts (jest, 4 cells) and ks1780-extract-pg-code-cannot-hang-a-webhook-patch.test.ts (jest, 8 cells). The third part of KS-1780, the catches in routes/adminConfig.ts, is a separate change and is not here. No tier timing or budget in these documents moves.

102. The ks968 integration suite’s loopback guard judges what the pg client will dial, and the file type-checks (KS-1494)

What this changes. KS-1494 items 1 and 4, test-only. The guard in services/auth/integration/ks968-platform-admin-seed-with-both-rows.integration.ts asked new URL(RAW) for the host and the database name. The pg client resolves the same string differently: a ?host= or ?port= in the query string overrides the authority, a DSN that names no port dials 5432, a unix-socket ?host=/path makes new URL throw, and hostaddr is ignored by pg but honoured by libpq. The suite truncates users and pii_subject_keys, so a guard that reads the wrong host is a guard that does not guard.
The guard now builds a pg Client from the DSN (no socket opens until connect()) and judges what it reports: a loopback host, a usable port that is not a shared-stack port (5432, 6432 and 6433, plus whatever docker-compose.yml publishes for Postgres and pgbouncer), and a database whose name starts with ks_. A DSN that names a hostaddr, in any case or percent-encoding, is refused, and so is one the client cannot parse. It never calls new URL, so no DSN shape escapes as a bare TypeError.
Same decision as KS 1340 (pull request 1790, head 3a9b1c121f6d), minus the two gaps its gate 8 found (KS 1795): 6433, the shared stack’s pgbouncer port, is refused, and the hostaddr test matches its key without regard to case or percent-encoding.
Item 4: the file’s 4 tsc errors (TS2493 x3 and TS2352 x1 on the err.mock.calls destructurings) are cleared by one named type, errorCalls, with no @ts-ignore. The four hooks moved into the describe of the six real-Postgres cells so the new guard cells run without a database. Items 2, 3 and 5 of KS-1494 and userRepo.ts are not touched.

tsc on the file (a scratch config that extends tsconfig.test.json and includes it): 4 errors at base, 0 now; eslint on the file: 0 errors, 0 warnings (planted controls: a type error reads 1 error, a lint violation 2 errors and 1 warning).
