103. /api/oauth/authorize refuses a scope that is not a string with 400 invalid_request, instead of a 500 (KS-1219)

What this changes. Behaviour change: on the authorize route a scope that is present and is not a string now answers 400 invalid_request. That covers an ARRAY (a repeated query parameter ?scope=a&scope=b, or a JSON array in the POST body), which used to answer 500 server_error because parseScopeString calls .split on it; and a JSON null, 0 or false, which parseScopeString treated as an absent scope (the default allow-list, KS-822 F-4) and which now answer 400 too. Only a JSON body can carry those scalars; query-string and form values are strings or arrays. Wednesday accepted the tightening on 2026-10-28. In services/auth/src/routes/oauth.ts, resolveAuthorizeClient returns the existing invalid_request message (description “scope must be a single space- or comma-separated string”) before it calls parseScopeString, so no published message changes. A local model (the Spark, DeepSeek V4 Flash, pass ks_1219_p1) wrote the patch; its checker passed 7 of 7 and the patch is byte-identical to the drafter’s golden. It was applied here strictly and unchanged.
The product file changes +10 / −0 (a three-line comment and a seven-line guard). The new test is services/auth/src/__tests__/ks1219-authorize-refuses-an-array-valued-scope.test.ts (vitest, 9 cells), which drives the real router on a loopback listener with the same mocks as ks804-authorize-get-post-agree-per-rule.test.ts. Its cells cover the array carriers (R1 to R3) and the JSON null, 0 and false edge (R4, three cells, added at the merge prep on the gate’s note), with three controls (C1 to C3). This is an authentication-surface change. No tier timing or budget in these documents moves.

104. services/auth AppError subclasses keep their own prototype, so the weak-password 422 now carries its feedback in the published array shape (KS-1467, the services/auth half)

What this changes. Behaviour change: the three weak-password 422 answers of services/auth (registration and password reset in routes/auth.ts, lines 204 and 822 at the base, and change-password in routes/users.ts, line 993) now carry error.details as an array with one { code: ‘custom’, path: [<field>], message } per feedback line, path being [‘password’] or, for change-password, [‘newPassword’]. That is the shape the published 422 already promises (ValidationErrorResponse: details is a ZodIssue-compatible array), so the OpenAPI schema is not widened and no client meets a new shape. Round 1 of this change sent { feedback: [...] }, an object; the tier-1 gate (gate 9, finding 1799-1) found that, and Wednesday ruled round 2 (2026-10-28 14:57:54Z): conform to the published contract. Line 173 of routes/auth.ts (a role not permitted on /register) has no details and is unchanged. Cause: the AppError constructor in services/auth/src/middleware/errorHandler.ts ended with Object.setPrototypeOf(this, AppError.prototype), which reset every subclass instance to the base prototype, so err instanceof ValidationError was always false and the handler’s own if (err instanceof ValidationError && err.details) branch (line 296) never ran. The constructor now uses new.target.prototype (one line), and a stale comment above the 503 check in passwordLoginGate.ts is reworded. The feedback is a list of fixed strings built by checkPasswordStrength (only the minimum length is interpolated), so it cannot echo the candidate password; cell N1 proves that through the real helper, class and handler, and the E cells prove it through the three real routes. Wednesday accepted the visible change on 2026-10-28, on that one condition. A local model (the Spark, DeepSeek V4 Flash, pass ks_1467_p1) wrote the first patch (the prototype line and the comment); its checker passed 7 of 7 and it is byte-identical to the drafter’s golden and was applied unchanged. The round 2 helper and the route cells were written by the raise seat.
Product: errorHandler.ts +7 / −1 (the constructor line, and the new weakPasswordIssues helper beside ValidationError), routes/auth.ts +3 / −2 and routes/users.ts +2 / −2 (the three sites and their imports), passwordLoginGate.ts +2 / −2 (comment only). Tests: ks1467-auth-app-error-subclasses-keep-their-own-prototype.test.ts (vitest, 35 cells: the Spark’s 34 plus N1, which round 2 moves to the array shape) and, new in round 2, ks1467-the-weak-password-422-through-the-real-routes.test.ts (vitest, 10 cells: S for each of the three routes parses the 422 through the published schema, E for each fails if the submitted password appears anywhere in the response, B for each is a control, V0 is a control on the schema). This is the services/auth half; the packages/shared half is a separate change. No tier timing or budget in these documents moves.

105. originate adminConfig.ts: fifteen catch conditions can no longer be hung by a hostile thrown value (KS-1780, part 2)

What this changes. KS-1780, part 2: fifteen catch blocks in services/originate/src/routes/adminConfig.ts tested err?.message?.includes(...) or err?.code BEFORE they reached fail500. That read touches the thrown value itself, so a revoked Proxy, or an object whose message getter throws, made the read throw from inside the catch: the handler’s promise rejected and the request got no answer at all (the KS 1772 shape, one step earlier; fail500 already survives such a value). Two small helpers, errorMessageIncludes and isMissingTableError, now do those reads inside a try and return false when the value cannot be inspected, so such a value is not a “table missing” or “unique constraint” error and falls through to fail500, which answers the constant 500. Thirteen of the fifteen sites are the missing-table check (does not exist or code 42P01); the other two are one message check on POST /document-types (unique constraint) and one on GET /rights-holders/:id/documents (does not exist only). For a readable value nothing changes, with one strictness: the helpers compare with === true. A local model (the Spark, DeepSeek V4 Flash, pass ks_1780_p2_admin) wrote the patch; its checker passed 7 of 7 and it is byte-identical to the drafter’s golden. It was applied here strictly and unchanged.
adminConfig.ts changes +36 / −15 (the two helpers and the fifteen replaced conditions). The new test is ks1780-admin-config-catches-cannot-hang-on-a-hostile-throw.test.ts (jest, 21 cells): A1 and A2 on four GET routes (eight cells), C1 to C3 on the same four routes (twelve controls) and S1, a source-text pin. 108. A did:jwk that carries a private key is refused: the guard on actorDid and orgDid (KS-1175)

What this changes. Kam’s ruling of 2026-10-29 19:51:25 AEDT on the card secuura-ks1175-private-jwk-guard-1029, option a, “Add a narrow guard before deploying”: “decode the did:jwk value only to refuse private-key members (d, p, q, dp, dq, qi, k), with a 400 and a clear message. Nothing else about the JWK is checked.” A did:jwk is a public key by construction, and what is anchored is public and permanent, so a JWK that carries private-key material (RFC 7518 and RFC 8037: d for EC, OKP and RSA; p, q, dp, dq, qi for RSA; k for oct) must never reach the chain. The shape pattern from the previous entry cannot see inside the payload, so the validator now decodes a did:jwk far enough to read its member NAMES and refuses it with a 400 (zod issue code custom, message starting Invalid DID, naming the members found and carrying no value) when any of the seven is a top-level member.
The one design choice the ruling implies, and the strictness behind it. A payload that is not unpadded base64url of a JSON object is refused too (an undecodable did:jwk is not a public key; Wednesday’s reading of the ruling). The alphabet is checked BEFORE the decode, because Node’s base64url decoder silently skips any other character, and the DID pattern admits ., : and %: a lenient decode could read a different JWK from the one a strict resolver sees. The guard steps aside for a value the shape checks already refuse (over the cap, outside the alphabet), so a bad value is refused once, for its own reason, and it applies to the did:jwk: prefix only: did:key and did:web carry no decodable JWK and are unchanged. Nothing else is read: no kty, no curve, no key use, no key length.
Changed: anchorSchema.ts (+52 / −2: the exported DID_JWK_PRIVATE_MEMBERS, didJwkRefusal, a superRefine on didField, and the posture sentence, which used to say K never decodes the JWK); anchoring.openapi.ts (both DID descriptions carry the rule, built from DID_JWK_PRIVATE_MEMBERS so the text cannot drift); docs/openapi/secuura-api.yaml (generated, +5 / −2: the two description strings); docs/VOCABULARY.md; ks1175-identity-anchoring.test.ts (+168 / −35). Read and left: didField is module-local and only ever .optional()-ed into identitySchema, so the repo rule that base string schemas stay chainable (.regex(), not .refine()) is not engaged; z.infer still reads string. anchorReadback.ts imports only IDENTITY_FIELDS, so reading back an anchor validates nothing. The route answers a refusal as 400 Validation failed with zod’s issues, which carry no input value.
This supersedes two sentences of section 106 (the previous entry for this ticket). That entry says K “never decodes the JWK” and that the pattern admits “not only valid base64url JSON”. Since this change K decodes a did:jwk to read its member names, and a did:jwk whose payload is not base64url JSON is refused. The pattern itself is unchanged. A deployed did:jwk was never reachable before this guard: the widening of section 106 is merged and not deployed.

108.1 What proves it

51 new cells, each red against a mutant that should break it. In one new describe block of ks1175-identity-anchoring.test.ts, for each of actorDid and orgDid: each of the seven private members refused on a P-256 public JWK carrying it (one issue, on the field, code custom, message ending in the member’s name, and neither the value nor the payload anywhere in the serialised refusal); a real P-256 private JWK (RFC 7515 A.3) and an Ed25519 one (RFC 8037 A.1) refused; every private member present listed in the guard’s order; a unicode-escaped d read as the member d; an Ed25519 public JWK (RFC 8037 A.2) accepted and kept verbatim; a public JWK whose kid reads “d” and use reads “k” accepted (names, not values); a JSON object without kty accepted (nothing else is checked); a payload that is text, an array, null, a string or a number refused; base64url letters that decode to non-JSON bytes refused; a stray ., : or % in an otherwise public payload refused; a private JWK over the cap refused once, as too_big; did:key, did:web and a did:web path that reads did:jwk: accepted; and a documented limit, a differently-cased D and a nested d accepted. One more cell sends a private did:jwk inside an otherwise valid identity block and expects the whole request refused on identity.actorDid. The file reads 117 cells, was 66; the four named anchoring files read 211/211 (were 160/160).
Three cells of the previous entry were rebuilt, not added. Their payloads (all A, the whole alphabet) are not JSON, which the guard now refuses, so each would have gone red for the wrong reason. They now carry public JWKs that decode: the - and _ cell (ASCII > and ? in the kid encode to those two characters), the exactly-512 cell, and the over-the-cap cell, which is now 514 characters because no payload that decodes is 513 long (base64url lengths are never 1 mod 4); the exact 512 / 513 boundary is still pinned by the existing did:web arm.

Not run: the four platform suites (Schemathesis, Akto, Playwright, Performance/k6), any stack or database (the ks1385 integration files need one), Docker, a Node 24 LTS run, and any anchor of a did:jwk on any network or box. Not deployed. The spec pattern still describes a did:jwk that the runtime now refuses (a pattern cannot express “decodes to a JSON object without a private member”): a Schemathesis positive case generated from the pattern could meet a 400 on these two fields, and POST /api/anchors has no per-operation override in schemathesis.toml, so the default positive-case statuses (no 400) apply to it. That is unmeasured here, and widening an expected-status list is masking by that file’s own rule, so it is for the owner of the suite to decide.
Limits, stated and pinned, not endorsed. Names are matched exactly and only at the top level, so a differently-cased D and a nested d are not refused; a consumer that reads JWK members case-insensitively would see the first as the member d. The RSA member oth (other primes) is not in Kam’s list; a JWK that carries it also carries d and is refused on that. Whether Platform S can ever put a private member in a did:jwk it sends is unmeasured, as is how many private-key shapes real wallets emit.
A private key that reaches this guard has already travelled from Platform S through the gateway and originate. Whether any of them logs a request body on a 400 is not measured here; the anchoring service itself returns no input value.

111. Platform S’s signature hash is accepted on the sign verb, anchored verbatim and read back (KS-1454)

What this changes. In anchorSchema.ts the anchor request’s metadata gains an optional signatureHash: the plain SHA-256 of Platform S’s detached .p7s, exactly 64 lowercase hex characters. A refinement answers 400 when it arrives on any verb but sign, or with no verb, so a stray hash is never anchored as if it named a signature. On a sign anchor it is written into the anchored metadata payload verbatim, beside documentType.
In anchorReadback.ts a new pure function anchorSignatureHashView reads the string back from secuura.signatureHash; a value that is not a string, or no key at all (every anchor that predates the field), reads null. The verify-by-hash response builder includes it, and in index.ts the GET /api/anchors/:id handler spreads the same view (one import and one spread line). B1 and B2: the view returns the hash from a database-form payload and from one that went through the chain codec. 113. Another tenant’s anchor reads exactly as an absent one on GET /api/anchors/:id and /document/:documentId (KS-1822)

What this changes. The two anchor reads had no tenant check: behind jwtAuthenticate() only, with unscoped row reads, so any authenticated caller read another tenant’s anchor (content hash, transaction, anchored identity and signature hash) by anchor id, through the document-id fallback, or by document id. 117. The anchor retry route checks who may re-anchor, and refuses a revoked or deleted document (KS-1814)

What this changes. POST /api/documents/:id/anchor (originate routes/documents.ts, the retry route) spends an anchoring fee and rewrites the document’s status. Before this change it checked only authentication and the caller’s tenant. It now refuses, in this order and every time before the anchoring call: a caller with neither a document-write role nor the documents:write scope (403, before the document is read); a caller who is not a platform admin, the owner or the creating connector (the same 404 an absent document gets); a revoked or deleted document (400). The write now passes preserveTerminalStatuses, as the create path does.
Platform S keeps working: its connector key carries documents:write and is the creating connector of the documents it re-anchors, ownerless ones and /version-minted children included (cells P1, the Platform S cell, and P1b, P2, P4). The S organisation-merge edge is refused, as Kam ruled on 2026-10-20 (card secuura-ks1688-org-merge-edge-which-side-1020, option a). An OWNER-role user re-anchors only its own documents (cells Q4, Q4b, Q5).

118. The NFT certificate list answers only the verified caller’s rows: the query string can no longer name the owner (KS-1836)

What this changes. GET /api/nft/certificates took its owner from the query string (?userId=, default 'user-id'), and a ?walletAddress= selector read any wallet with no owner check. Both mint paths stamp every record 'user-id', so a bare list by any authenticated caller returned every recorded NFT across users and tenants, each with its encryptedKey. A new nftReadGate.ts (+95 lines) holds two pure functions: readerIdentity (the caller’s trimmed userId, or null when it is absent, not a string, blank, or any spelling of the legacy 'user-id') and selectReadableCertificates (only rows whose userId equals the owner, exactly and case-sensitively; each selector can only narrow).
The list handler in nft.routes.ts (+22 -9, plus one import line) reads the owner from req.user, which jwtAuthenticate() sets. A caller with no usable identity gets 403 and no service method runs. Otherwise the service readers run unchanged (the wallet query when a string wallet selector is given, else the user query with the owner id, never the query string’s), and the result goes through the gate. count is the filtered length. An empty selector counts as absent; a selector that is not a string (a repeated parameter) matches nothing and never reaches SQL.
A refusal reads as empty: a selector naming another user’s wallet or id gets the same 200 { certificates: [], count: 0 } a caller with no rows gets, byte for byte, never a 403, so it says nothing about what the wallet holds. One warn line names the caller’s owner id, the selector and the counts; the response names no other owner, and no log carries a key. No spec change: the route already declares 200 and 403 and no query parameters.
Two new test files. ks1836-nft-list-owner-bound.test.ts (+334 lines, 24 cells) mounts the real router on an express app over an ephemeral port, with a test-only middleware standing in for jwtAuthenticate(). The real minting service runs against a fake table that answers its four SQL shapes and throws on any other; its in-memory Map is real (fresh modules per cell); the chain module and the Blockfrost verifier are test doubles. ks1836-nft-read-gate.test.ts (+72 lines, 7 cells) unit-tests the two functions.

Red on develop’s handler, red under 17 mutants, green with the gate. The route file on develop’s nft.routes.ts: 17 of 24 red. R1 returned the legacy row; R2, R4, R5, R6, R13, R14 and R15 returned another owner’s rows; R8 to R12 answered 200 instead of 403; R16’s bodies carried another owner’s id and wallet; R17 logged nothing; R18 sent an array to the wallet query; R20 read the legacy owner for empty selectors. Green on develop, as controls: R3 and R7 (the caller’s own selectors), R19 (the published list schema), C1 (the 500 envelope), C2 (the by-id route still serves another owner’s row, a known gap pinned), C3 (/tiers) and C4 (no live chain path). The gate file does not load on develop (the module is absent), so its 7 cells did not run there. With the change: 31 of 31 pass.
17 mutants, one at a time, each parsed with esbuild before it ran (a planted unclosed brace was refused), restored with git checkout and a sha256 read back equal to HEAD: the gate dropped from both branches; the owner taken from ?userId; the wallet branch, then the user branch, skipping the gate; owner-or-wallet instead of owner-and-wallet; each of the four terms of readerIdentity removed on its own (user present, a string, not blank, not the legacy owner) and the legacy check made exact; a case-insensitive owner match; 403 on a withheld row; the owner id added to the body; count of the unfiltered list; the owner read from tenantId or organizationId; and each empty-selector rule dropped. 17 of 17 killed.

124. Two comments in the anchoring reconciler now match the code, and the did:jwk shape test pins six more refused characters (KS-1816, KS-1830)

What this changes. Comments only in Blockchain/Dev/services/anchoring/src/reconciler.ts (+12 / -4 lines, three hunks). The header property no longer says a chain-provider error always leaves the row untouched: it says so only below the give-up age, and that past it (strictly older than the give-up age) the same error is read as absence and the row is marked failed (KS 1810). The MIN_AGE comment no longer says the live loop touches updated_at as it goes: it says the confirmation poll writes nothing between submitted and confirmed, so a row the live loop is still polling can pass MIN_AGE. The catch comment inside the loop now says what reaches it: the catch is reached when the chain check or the status write rejects; the production chain check catches a provider error itself and answers not-confirmed, so an outage is decided by the header rule above, not by the catch.

What this changes. Akto 2.41.6 → 2.42.6: both 2.42.6_local tags were pushed to Docker Hub on 2026-10-30; 2.42.3 and 2.42.5 are dashboard-only. Akto released v2.42.7 at 09:29Z the same day, but at 10:59Z only the dashboard had 2.42.7_local (testing: 404), so 2.42.6 is still the latest matched pair; Peter ruled to stay on 2.42.6 for this change.
The minimum. Every npm range’s floor is the version installed (dependencyFloors.test.ts), and npm run start refuses an AKTO_IMAGE_VERSION / AKTO_DASHBOARD_VERSION / AKTO_TESTING_VERSION below the pin, from the shell or .env (scripts/assert-akto-version-floor.sh). A newer override is still allowed.
The tooling. update-akto-images.sh reads up to five pages of tags per image (a note when it stopped early but still found the pair; a warning when it did not) and names package.json as the pin; aktoPinDocMirrors.test.ts checks the 14 prose copies of the pin; systemTest/CLAUDE.md names the right test for each copy; and the harness re-uses one dashboard login per process and keeps a per-slot ledger of login times (no token), refusing at once, with docker restart <dashboard> as the remedy, when Akto’s 10-per-hour budget is spent. The ledger follows Akto’s own refill: Refill.intervally(10, Duration.ofHours(1)) in its RateLimitFilter (v2.42.6, identical at v2.41.6) puts all 10 back at once on each full hour from the first login after the dashboard starts, so the ledger counts those hours, not a sliding 60 minutes.
New templates and categories are scanned. A stale template catalog now blocks scanning: test:pr, test:pre-merge and test:security run check-test-ids first, and npm run start exits 1 at its end. It used to warn only, because CI blocked staleness, and CI is retired. test:security selects every catalogued template, so a regenerated catalog is all a new template or category needs. At 2.42.6 the catalog is byte-identical to 2.41.6’s: 213 ids, 21 categories.

128. The single-use MFA backup-code burn removes exactly the matched stored hash in one conditional UPDATE, so two concurrent sign-ins cannot spend one code twice (KS-1848, KS-1849)

What this changes. Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/repositories/userRepo.ts gains consumeBackupCode(id, storedHash): one UPDATE users SET mfa_backup_codes = array_remove(mfa_backup_codes, $1), updated_at = NOW() WHERE id = $2 AND $1 = ANY(mfa_backup_codes), run under the tenant updateUser resolves. A row count above 0 is read back under the same scope, as updateUserOrThrow did. A row count of 0 is re-read through the pre-auth carve-out: a stored set that still exists and lacks the hash means another request spent the code or replaced the set (a regenerate); no row, a NULL set, or the hash still stored is the 503 it always was. updateUser itself is unchanged.
services/passwordLoginGate.ts, the burn block only: the gate burns the stored hash that matched, never an index; a burn that lost the race answers the uniform refusal and counts once in the lockout, which is what a replay of a spent code answers; the request’s own copy of the codes is trimmed only after a confirmed burn. Before KS-1848 the gate spliced the code out of its snapshot and wrote the whole array back by id. Gate 38 F1: the comment above that refusal used to say a lost race “is no oracle”; it now says that status, body and lockout count are identical to a replay of a spent code but time is not (a lost race answers about 30 ms sooner, because verifyBackupCode returns at the first matching hash). Comment only.
Kept as ruled: the burn still comes before the credential, and a burn that cannot be confirmed still answers 503 with the KS-1188 F3 wording (card secuura-ks1188-burnt-backup-code-wording-1005, choice a). No migration: mfa_backup_codes is a nullable text[] with no index, and the only CHECK on users is the status vocabulary (read on the throwaway database below).
Tests: a new unit file ks1848-backup-code-burn-is-conditional.test.ts (18 cells), a new real-Postgres file integration/ks1848-backup-code-burn-concurrency.integration.ts (13 cells: the first 8, then B0 to B2 and L3, L4 from gate 38’s follow-ups), and the new function added to the userRepo mock of ks781-login-authorize-agree.test.ts and ks781-oauth-authorize-mfa-bypass.test.ts. LEG 4 of the second now pins the door, the count and the burned hash, where it asserted only that updateUserOrThrow was called (KS-1849). ks1188-f3-a-spent-backup-code-503-says-so.test.ts and ks1052-backup-code-burn-cause-a.test.ts are untouched and green.

Real Postgres, untouched develop, 20 forced rounds per cell (an admin connection holds the row FOR UPDATE, the cell asserts both UPDATEs are queued on that lock in pg_stat_activity, then releases): the same code raced twice succeeded twice in 20 of 20 rounds; codes A and B raced left two codes stored and a spent code accepted again in 20 of 20; unforced (Promise.all) 20 of 20 for both; a burn racing a backup-code regenerate overwrote the new set in 20 of 20, and one racing an MFA disable left a code on the disabled account in 20 of 20. 129. Each PR adds its own docs fragment and one build step renders the two pages, so two PRs no longer conflict on them (KS-1887)

What this changes. Projects Documents/fragments/flow/ and Projects Documents/fragments/cheat/ hold head.html, tail.html, a frozen legacy/ directory (the 117 Flow entries and 112 Cheat Sheet entries on the pages at develop 9e1eb55fde53, with their literal numbers, in the pages’ own order) and one KS-NNNN-slug.html per new entry. A new Flow entry writes <!--n--> where its section number goes and <!--ref:NAME--> for another new entry’s number; the Cheat Sheet is unnumbered, so its fragments are plain HTML.
Blockchain/Dev/scripts/docs-fragments.mjs (no dependencies, no timestamps): check is the hard fragment lint (name, one entry per file, tag balance, tokens, no literal number in a new Flow entry, no token in a legacy file), the render passed through systemTest/__tests__/support/html_docs_check.mjs, and an advisory on how each committed page relates to the render; check --committed also needs both pages current; build --base <develop sha> rewrites the pages (refused unless that sha is an ancestor of HEAD, and never over content the fragments do not hold); build --out DIR is a preview; adopt [--from-ref REF [--against SHA]] turns an entry written by hand into a fragment; legacy-hash prints the pin.
Numbers: a new entry is numbered by the commit that first added it (git rev-list --first-parent order, ties by file name, an uncommitted file last), counting up from the highest literal number in the head and the legacy files; the build refuses a shallow clone. No PR rebuilds the committed pages: one separate docs-only push refreshes them after a batch of merges, so they may lag the fragments, and a hand edit of a page is an advisory with exit 0, never a stopped push.
Blockchain/Dev/scripts/__tests__/docs_fragments.test.sh sits in a root that run-shell-suites.sh already globs, so leg 12 finds it and leg 14 runs it. Not edited: .githooks/pre-push, any preflight leg, html_docs_check.mjs, html_docs_matrix.test.sh, check-stack-safety.sh. .claude/skills/secuura-test-discipline/SKILL.md: section 4 only.

129.1 What proves it

Byte-identical, with controls that can fail. The render equals the committed pages at develop 9e1eb55fde53: Flow sha256 62990735186b4659dccc5676e7b5261da43d45ba70adc2997e22accf87fdcd9c (904074 bytes) and Cheat Sheet c89d4c382a76678fa16697ce1c55c0ccbaccc4363da67b59858e466594c8ea19 (599851 bytes), each computed three ways: git show of that sha, build --out, and the file on disk. 117 Flow and 112 Cheat fragments equal the per-PR entries (124 − 7 head sections, and 112 − 0).
Planted change: one changed character in one legacy fragment makes the rendered hash differ from the committed page and check --committed exit 1; restored by content (a unique anchor, count 1) the file’s sha256 equals the original and check --committed exits 0 again. html_docs_check.mjs on both renders exits 0, and exits 1 with “prose outside a table” on a planted paragraph. html_docs_matrix.test.sh 18 of 18.
The collision is gone: two scratch branches each adding a different fragment merge with 0 conflict files and are numbered 129 and 130 by merge order; the same two edits made the old way (a section appended to each page) conflict in both pages (2 files).
Cells: docs_fragments.test.sh 81 cells, all passing, 14 s standalone. Mutants: 41 single-edit mutants of the script (each parsed first, its anchor counted once), every one killed by at least one cell. Sweeps left three alive along the way, rev-list without --first-parent under clock skew, a same-length edit of the head, and no stem check in adopt --against (a same-length edit of old text plus an appended entry would have been half-adopted), and they became cells B10, C5 and E15. The first run of the cells (61 of 64) also caught the tool calling an edited entry “hand-appended” and adopt writing a fragment from it; cells C3, E4 and E7c now hold that.
The transition, on real open PRs in detached scratch worktrees, nothing pushed: #1837 (1 Flow and 1 Cheat entry) 8 of 8 steps, #1857 (a stack: 4 and 4) 8 of 8, with every adopted entry equal byte for byte to the text in the PR’s own page; #1383 (rewrites page text) is refused as a hand step, as predicted. The first try on #1837 was refused too, because its page was stale; --against (cells E10 to E14) is the fix.

129.3 What this does not prove

The numbering and the process, not every history. Ordering by the first-add commit is proved on throwaway repos (squash shape, tie, merge-in shape, clock skew, delete and re-add, shallow clone), not on a long-lived develop. Two stacked PRs both converting the same base entry were not tested together (one stack member was tested alone); the names derive from the heading, so the files should be identical.
The committed pages lag the fragments until the first refresh; who runs it, and how often, is a process decision in SKILL.md, not code. A PR that edits existing page text, such as #1383, needs a hand step.
A push that touches only Projects Documents/ skips the pre-push gate, as a docs-only push does today, so a bad fragment merged that way fails leg 14 for the next code push until it is fixed.

130. Five admin-labelled routes now require a platform administrator, and a KYC reviewer may not review their own verification (KS-1845)

What this changes. Five routes that their own comments or the published spec call admin-only checked no role, so any signed-in caller could call them:
  • POST /api/kyc/:id/review, which decides a KYC verification and sets its level;
  • POST /api/governance/process-expired;
  • POST /api/delegations/admin/process-expired;
  • GET /api/stake/all;
  • GET /api/wallets/sessions.
Each now refuses, as its first step, any caller whose role does not pass the shared isPlatformRole (SYSTEM_ADMIN or SUPER_ADMIN, ASCII case fold only, a non-string refused). The refusal is the 403 the spec already declares: “Reviewer role required” for the review, “Admin role required” for the other four. Nothing the route does is reached on a refusal.
The review also refuses the verification’s own subject, even a platform administrator. That check refuses on equality, so a strict compare would fail open on any spelling difference: both ids are folded first, and an id that is missing or not a string is refused too (QA gate 42 found the bypass: an upper-case UUID in the row). Its role check runs before the body is parsed or the id is looked up, so a refused caller learns neither (no 400, no 404).
Five new test files (ks1845-*.test.ts, one per service, 72 cells: 24 for kyc and 12 for each of the other four). Three existing fixtures change their test principal only, with no assertion changed:
  • ks849-mock-timer-stale-write.test.ts: ADMIN to SYSTEM_ADMIN;
  • staking.test.ts: the stub role is SYSTEM_ADMIN inside the GET /api/stake/all describe only;
  • ks1410-delegations-process-expired-500.test.ts: role: SYSTEM_ADMIN added.
The spec is unchanged: all five operations already declared the 403.

131. The catch of KS-1844 GET /api/certifications/:id answers a thrown value it cannot read instead of leaving the request without a reply

What this changes.The catch of GET /api/certifications/:id in Blockchain/Dev/services/originate/src/routes/certifications.ts (about lines 1063 to 1095) read code, meta.code, error instanceof Error and error.message straight off the thrown value with no try of its own. A thrown value whose property read throws (a revoked Proxy, or an Error whose code or message getter throws) therefore threw inside the catch of an async Express 4 handler, and the request got no answer. The two reads are now each inside a try: a value that cannot be read is not a 22P02 and falls through to the constant 500 envelope, and the log reason is coerced to a string inside its own try (String() of the message, or of the value), with the fixed fallback unreadable thrown value when that cannot be done. +20 -3 in one file (QA gate 36, round 1, added the string coercion and the definite-assignment declaration).
Behaviour changes only for a thrown value that cannot be read: the request now gets the constant 500 where it got no answer. The 404 branch keeps the original expressions (error as { code?: string })?.code ?? (error as { meta?: { code?: string } })?.meta?.code and error instanceof Error && error.message.includes('22P02') byte for byte (each occurs once in the base and once now), only inside the new try, with the local renamed from pgCode to thrownCode and the condition split into an assignment and if (invalidId). The constant 500 line is untouched.
New test ks1844-get-certification-by-id-answers-a-hostile-throw.test.ts, 8 jest cells: D1 to D4 are RED (a revoked Proxy from getCertification, an Error whose code getter throws, an Error whose message getter throws, and an Error whose message is a revoked Proxy, each answered with the whole constant 500 envelope; D1, D3 and D4 also assert that the log reason is the fixed fallback text, a string; a request with no answer in 1500 ms is reported as the string NO ANSWER, so a hang is a red assertion and not a stuck run); C1 to C4 are controls (a bare 22P02, a 22P02 only in meta.code and a 22P02 only in the message text are still answered 404, and an ordinary Error is still answered 500 and logged by its message).
Scope: the whole ticket as far as its description goes (the unguarded reads at the catch), referenced as Refs. Not covered: a Prisma-shaped error with code: 'P2010', meta.code: '22P02' and no 22P02 in the message is answered 500, not 404, because a ?? b takes 'P2010'; this change preserves that behaviour (cell C2 pins meta.code with no own code) and does not alter it. A real Prisma P2010 raw-query error carries the code in its message (board ticket KS 1659 quotes a measured one), so on a real error the second test, error.message.includes('22P02'), already answers 404 and the shape needs a hand-built error.

131.1 What proves it

Against the round-1 product (before QA gate 36’s F1): 1 of 8 fails (D4: the logged reason is an object, not a string). With the catch changed: 8 of 8 pass. Two mutants gate 36 found surviving are now killed: M3 (the fallback log reason dropped to an empty string) fails 3 of 8 (D1, D3, D4) and M7 (the reason leaked into the 500 body) fails 5 of 8 (D1 to D4 and C4), each restored sha256-equal.

134. POST /api/workflows/escalate requires a platform administrator (KS-1881)

What this changes. The transfer service’s POST /api/workflows/escalate (services/transfer/src/routes/workflows.ts) runs processEscalations(), which escalates or times out every overdue approval step in every tenant. Its own comment called it an admin endpoint, but it checked no role and did not read the request, so any signed-in caller could run the sweep. It now answers 403 FORBIDDEN “Admin role required” before the sweep runs, unless the caller’s role passes the shared isPlatformRole (SYSTEM_ADMIN or SUPER_ADMIN, ASCII case fold, a non-string refused). That is the same shape as KS-1845’s /admin/process-expired. The sweep itself is unchanged: an admin sweep over every tenant is the intended shape (Wednesday’s D1 ruling, 2026-10-31).
Who is now refused. Any caller without a platform role. Nothing in the repo calls this route. The gateway proxies only /api/transfers and /api/delegations to transfer (proxy.ts:1106, :1113) and answers its own four /api/workflows paths from Redis (proxy.ts:1124-1149); no nginx or Caddy config routes to transfer, and compose publishes no transfer port. So the route is reachable only service-to-service inside the network (QA gate 53’s reading). Out-of-repo schedulers are not measured.

137. The gateway refuses a document create from a caller with no write role or scope before the approval workflow writes anything (KS-1871)

What this changes. The gateway handles POST /api/documents itself (services/api-gateway/src/routes/verification.ts). For a document type that requires approval, it called createWorkflowInstanceIfRequired, which stores a workflow instance and the submitted body as a pending document, and answered 201 pending_approval for any authenticated caller. The same caller on a non-gated type reached originate and got its 403. Before the workflow gate, the gateway now applies originate’s own create rule: a document-write role (ISSUER_ADMIN, ORG_ADMIN, SYSTEM_ADMIN or SUPER_ADMIN, ASCII case fold) OR the documents:write scope. A caller with neither gets originate’s exact 403 FORBIDDEN, “Forbidden: your role does not permit document creation”.
OWNER keeps its 201. Every OWNER login token carries documents:write (KS-151, the auth service’s getDefaultScopesForRole), and originate admits it through the scope arm. So the ticket’s “OWNER must get 403” holds only for an OWNER token without that scope, such as an OAuth mint. Refused now: VERIFIER, HOLDER, USER, ISSUER, ADMIN, no role, and a connector key whose only scope is the legacy register.
Where the gateway is stricter than originate. An array-valued role and a Unicode case-fold (a dotless i) are refused; originate’s String(role).toUpperCase() admits both (the KS-1591 class). No real token carries either. The role list is a gateway copy of originate’s DOCUMENT_WRITE_ROLES, and a drift cell fails if the two differ.
A connector set to bypass the workflow also bypasses this check (QA gate 56, F1): with workflowPolicy: 'bypass' it writes no workflow and is forwarded to originate, whose own create rule then decides (the gate measured the forward and read originate’s refusal from the code; no real originate was run).

140. vc-issuer catch blocks keep logging when the thrown value is unreadable (KS-1868, vc-issuer)

What this changes. Three catch blocks in Blockchain/Dev/services/vc-issuer: credentialRepo.loadFromDb, presentations.loadPresentationsFromDb and credentialRepo.ensureTable. Each read the thrown value with no guard (err instanceof Error ? err.message : String(err), or err?.message). If the thrown value is a revoked Proxy, or an Error whose message getter throws, that read throws inside the catch: the WARN is never logged and the caller gets a TypeError instead. Each read now sits in an inner try with the fallback 'unreadable thrown value'; the WARN text, its key and the value logged for any readable thrown value are unchanged. Product bytes: credentialRepo.ts +14/-2, presentations.ts +7/-1.
Eight new cells in two new test files (ks1868-credentialrepo-loadfromdb-unreadable-throw.test.ts, 5 cells, +93 lines; ks1868-presentations-load-unreadable-throw.test.ts, 3 cells, +60 lines). Per site: a control that an ordinary Error still logs its message (C1; C2 for the table check), and red cells that a revoked Proxy (R1; R3 for the table check) and an Error with a throwing message getter (R2) log the constant reason. loadFromDb and loadPresentationsFromDb are two held Spark passes (O35-P1, O35-P2) applied with strict git apply --check -p1 (rc 0 on both, and rc 1 on a copy with one context line's content corrupted). ensureTable is the same shape written by hand, the one hand edit; it keeps err?.message semantics, so a thrown string or undefined still logs undefined.

143. Anchor status writes say how many rows they matched, the flat anchor create answers the anchoring time it will put on chain, originate no longer writes the anchoring service’s table, and the reconciler fails a row only after 24 h without a write and two answered “not found” passes (KS-1384 F-a)

What this changes.The row-count builder. services/anchoring/src/anchorStatusUpdate.ts: the status UPDATE builder gains expectStatus (one value, or a list read as status = ANY(...)) and expectTransactionHash (null means IS NULL, never = NULL). The body of dbUpdateAnchorStatus moves into an exported runAnchorStatusUpdate, which resolves to the matched row count, or to null when the write did not run or its result is unknown. The reconciler (below) reads the count; the submitter still ignores it (KS-1384 F0 is the first there).
One Date per request. POST /api/anchors takes one Date and uses it for the payload’s anchored timestamp and the row’s created_at. The 202 gains payloadTimestamp: the timestamp inside the payload the row holds after the upsert, read in the upsert’s own RETURNING, so a repeat request whose KS-1385 overwrite was declined reports the kept payload’s time. GET /api/anchors/:id gains the same field from the stored payload (null when it carries none). The published spec adds the field to the 202 schema (additive).
originate stops writing anchor_store. saveAnchorToDb in services/originate/src/routes/anchors.ts is removed with its two calls. It wrote the anchoring service’s anchor id into transaction_hash, a confirmed_at of now, and updated_at = NOW() over the row anchoring owns. The non-production “anchoring unreachable” 202 no longer says the request was persisted locally.
The reconciler’s give-up (KS-1808, KS-1810). services/anchoring/src/reconciler.ts: the 24 h window runs from the row’s last write (updated_at), not created_at, so a re-armed old row is no longer failed at its first pass. A row is failed only after TWO consecutive passes past the window in which the chain ANSWERED “not found” (the polled count of waitForConfirmation); a pass the provider could not answer never fails a row and starts the count again, as does a thrown check or a new hash on the row. The count is in memory, keyed by anchor id and hash, so a restart can only delay a failed write.
Guarded reconciler writes. Each confirmed or failed write expects the status set the pass selected (pending, submitted, submitting) and the hash it read, and only a write that matched its row (1) is counted; 0 (the row moved: a re-anchor or a final status) and null (the write did not run) are logged and left.
Comments and two pins. The reconciler header now states the new rule; its MIN_AGE comment (KS-1816) is kept, because it is still true; its catch comment says a provider outage is decided by the “could not ask” branch. ks1816-reconciler-comments-match-the-code.test.ts is rewritten in the same commit: R1 pins the new header sentence, C2 pins the updated_at give-up line; R2, C1 and C3 are unchanged. A comment in dbPersistAnchor named its two callers in call form, which the KS-1385 W1 source pin counted as two more calls (78 of 79 green); it now names them in words.

143.1 What proves it

Red at the base, green after, every mutant killed by its own cell.Unit, part 1 (ks1384-fa-row-count-builder.test.ts, 18 cells: (b1) the WHERE clauses, (c1) count or null, (pt) the payload reader, (wu) the builder stamps the Date it is given). Against develop’s modules: 18 of 18 red. Real-copy control: green.
Unit, the reconciler (ks1384-fa-reconciler-give-up-and-answered-passes.test.ts, 13 cells: (r) the window runs from the last write, (t) only answered passes count and the count restarts, (r3s) every write expects what it read and only a 1 is counted). Against develop’s reconciler.ts: 13 of 13 red. Real-copy control: green. The existing ks584-reconciler.test.ts “fails a real tx absent past the window” cell now runs two passes and checks the guard (6 of 6 green).
Real Postgres (ks1384-fa-one-date-per-request.integration.test.ts, 3 cells: (b2) the expectations executed, (w) 202 payloadTimestamp = stored timestamp = created_at, (w2) a declined overwrite reports the kept time; against develop: 3 of 3 red. ks1384-fa-reconciler-writes.integration.test.ts, 3 cells: (r2) a not-yet pass writes nothing, (r3) a row re-anchored during the chain check is not confirmed over, and a control; against develop’s reconciler: (r3) red, (r2) and the control green, (r2) red by its mutant). Real-copy controls: green.
originate (ks1384-fa-anchor-routes-write-no-anchor-row.test.ts, 3 cells (sa)): both routes reach anchoring and call prisma.$executeRaw zero times. Against develop’s route: 3 of 3 red. Real-copy control: green.
Mutants, each parsed before it ran and each killed only by its own cell: (b1) drop the expectStatus clause, 3 red; (b1) = $n for a null hash, 1 red; (c1) the catch returns 0, 1 red; (c1) resolve to undefined, 3 red; (pt) read a created-at field, 1 red; (wu) the builder ignores the Date it is given, 1 red; (b2) = NULL on Postgres, 1 red; (w) a distinct instant for the payload, 1 red; (w2) answer the incoming timestamp, 1 red; (sa) a write put back in /submit, 1 red; (sa) the old message, 1 red; (r) read created_at, 1 red; (r2) touch the row inside the window, 1 red; (r3) drop expectTransactionHash on Postgres, 1 red; (r3s) drop expectTransactionHash, 2 red; (r3s) drop expectStatus, 2 red; (r3s) count whatever the write returned, 1 red; (t) treat every not-confirmed pass as answered, 2 red; (t) fail on the first answered pass, 6 red (five (t) cells and the (r) cell that asserts the second pass, the same rule); (t) count by anchor id alone, 1 red; (t) no reset on an errored pass, 1 red; (t) no reset on a thrown check, 1 red.
The KS-1816 pin, both ways (each run on a scratch copy): the rewritten pin is 5 of 5 green on this reconciler.ts and 2 of 5 red (R1, C2) on develop’s; the pin as develop has it is 2 of 5 red (R1, C2) on this file and 5 of 5 green on develop’s.
Two existing files updated by part 1: ks1822-a-foreign-tenants-anchor-reads-as-absent.test.ts deep-equals the whole GET body, so its expected body gains payloadTimestamp: null (6 of 12 red without it); ks1293-originate-suite-is-hermetic.test.ts lists the new originate file in its manifest (MANIFEST-DRIFT red without it).

143.3 What this does not prove

Stated, not claimed.That the old two-new Date() shape ever produced different instants on a box: it differs only when the two calls straddle a millisecond, which a real-route cell cannot force. Cell (wu) pins the deterministic half and cell (w)’s mutant passes a distinct instant.
How a real provider behaves in an outage: the cells feed polled and errored counts; that the production check reports polled: 0 when every attempt threw is read from cardano/confirmation.ts, not measured against Blockfrost.
That two answered passes are enough on a congested chain: the count is the design’s choice, and a restart resets it (it can only delay a failed write).
The four platform suites, a running stack, Node 24 (LTS), and any box: not run here.

145. Billing’s customer, invoice and payment-method routes admit only the customer’s owner or a platform administrator (KS-1888)

What this changes. Twelve billing routes took a Stripe customer, invoice or payment-method id from the caller and acted on it with no check of who was asking: read or change any customer, spend its certification credits, list or detach its payment methods, read its invoices. POST /billing/customers also returned any existing customer to whoever posted its email, and PUT /billing/customers/:id let a caller write metadata.certificationCredits, which is where the balance lives.
The rule (the coordinator’s D1–D4, 2026-10-31): a caller may act on a customer when they are a platform administrator (the shared isPlatformRole, as KS-1850) or its owner: metadata.userId equals the caller’s userId, both non-empty strings, exact compare, and where the customer records metadata.tenantId it equals the caller’s. An invoice or payment method belongs to the owner of its customer; with no customer, or on a customer with no recorded owner, it is platform administrators only. Tenant roles get nothing beyond their own customer.
A refused caller gets the route’s own 404, byte-identical to an unknown id; no Stripe write or listing runs and nothing is logged. GET /customers/:id/credits now answers 404 for an unknown id too (it read as a zero balance). POST /customers takes the owner and tenant from the token, refuses a body userId that is not the caller’s with 403 (a platform administrator may create for another user), and returns an existing customer only to someone who may act on it; anyone else gets a new customer of their own. PUT refuses certificationCredits, userId and tenantId in metadata with 400, for everyone. GET /customers/by-email moved above GET /customers/:id: below it, Express sent /customers/by-email to the :id handler, so it never ran.
A customer created before this change carries whatever userId its creator posted, and the check trusts it. That is a limit of the fix, not a finding: there is no other owner record to check against.

145.1 What proves it

Red at develop, green after, every mutant killed. Red-first at develop df99b04720b8: 102 of the 192 route cells red, exactly the designed set:
  • on eleven routes, the seven refusals (another user, the owner under another tenant, a tenant administrator, a customer with no owner, no principal, no userId, a numeric userId);
  • on by-email, the six admissions, because the route never ran (its refusals were green only for that reason);
  • an unknown id on /credits; the two objects with no customer; six outage cells; five POST /customers cells; five reserved-key cells.
The 90 green: the admissions and unknown-id answers on eleven routes, the seven by-email refusals above, and seven controls (a platform administrator on an object with no customer, three POST /customers cells, an ordinary metadata key). A second file runs the new Stripe lookups against a mocked SDK: 18 of 19 red at develop (the methods did not exist), the 19th a control.
Whole billing suite with the change (vitest --maxWorkers=3): 13 files / 324 of 324, twice. The KS-445 and KS-421 harnesses gained a stand-in caller and lookup doubles that return that caller’s own customer, and three injection lines in KS-445 now target listCustomersByEmail, the call that replaced findCustomerByEmail; no assertion changed.
Mutants: 26 of 26 killed, each with the cells it names. Twenty in the routes: the owner compare dropped; the tenant compare dropped; a customer with no recorded tenant refused to its owner; a tenant administrator admitted; a platform administrator refused; an unowned customer or object admitted; a numeric userId coerced; 403 for 404; the reason logged; a reserved key allowed; the body userId trusted; an existing customer returned to anyone; by-email back below :id; a tenant recorded for someone else’s customer; the lookup swallowing an outage; the invoice route’s check bypassed; the check after the spend; the /credits check removed; everyone refused. Six in the lookups: every error read as missing; each of the three “does not exist” signals dropped in turn; a deleted customer returned; Stripe’s first match only.
tsc --noEmit over billing’s own config: 0 errors. With the test files in the program: the same 10 errors as at develop (TS1378 in six existing test files, TS6196, TS18046), none in this change; a planted error is reported. eslint on the six changed files: 0 errors; the 2 warnings are on unchanged lines that develop has too; a planted file raised two rules.

147. The GitHub sign-in adapter refuses a token answer that has no access token, before it calls /user (KS-1792)

What this changes.A sign-in adapter behaviour change. Blockchain/Dev/services/auth/src/providers/social/github.ts, +8/-2. GitHub answers a bad or expired sign-in code with HTTP 200 and an {error, error_description} body, so the adapter’s !ok branch never saw it: it read access_token unchecked and called /user with Bearer undefined, relying on GitHub answering 401 (then Failed to fetch GitHub user profile). It now refuses a token answer whose access_token is not a non-empty string, or that carries an error field, before any profile call, with GitHub token exchange failed (no access token). It logs a warning with the provider’s error string cut to 80 characters. A good token answer and the existing non-2xx refusal are unchanged.
New test ks1792-github-refuses-a-token-answer-without-an-access-token.test.ts, 8 cells, with fetch replaced by a recording stub (no socket): R1 a 200 bad_verification_code error answer, R2 a 200 empty object, R3 a 200 answer whose access_token is not a string, each refused with /user never called; and, added at merge prep (gate 33 F1, F2), R4 a 200 answer whose access_token is an empty string and R5 a 200 answer that carries an error next to a string access_token, each refused with /user never called, and R6 the refusal logs only the error code (the token in the answer is in no logger channel); C1 a good token answer still signs in with the Bearer token; C2 a non-2xx token answer is still the status-only failure. The message a signing-in user sees for a bad code changes from the /user failure text to the token-exchange text: read from the code, not measured end to end.
